documents.title: Building the Tools for Private and Local-First Coordination
documents.description: Why PriFi needs more than a private blockchain
documents.body: Privacy in the world of blockchain and decentralised finance has been almost entirely focused on blockchain mechanisms, which is understandable enough, since that is where value transfers are settled and where a permanent public record forms. However, reducing exposure here still leaves most of a transaction’s supply chain unprotected.  Finding a counterparty, establishing their identity, and agreeing on terms all happen somewhere else, on infrastructure that is leaky and vulnerable to exposure. By the time a shielded transfer is executed on the blockchain, there have already been myriad opportunities to expose data around it. PriFi is an approach to taking privacy across the whole lifecycle of a transaction seriously, reducing exposure every step of the way. If you’re new to PriFi, we recommend  reading this introductory explainer before continuing with this more technical article. In this article, we refresh our memories on the concept of PriFi before drilling into the first few stages of a transaction’s lifecycle and how Logos is building infrastructure that aims to reduce your exposure when coordinating a transaction. To understand more about how transactions can leak information, download  Logos Basecamp and install  Muster , an application built on Logos by Dr Corey Petty, to demonstrate how transactions can leak information throughout their lifecycle. What is PriFi? PriFi (private finance) is an infrastructure design philosophy that aims to make every step of the transaction supply chain private, secure, and immune to leakage. It unlocks elective disclosure, allowing people or institutions to choose how much or how little about their transactions they want to share. It is not a single solution and is best understood as an ongoing principle of development for sovereign and privacy-preserving infrastructure – a north star guiding the course for building parallel systems that hand true control to their users. The lifecycle of a transaction can be seen as seven distinct stages: # Stage Operation 1 Discovery Finding who has what you want 2 Diligence Verifying they are who they claim 3 Negotiation Agreeing on price and terms 4 Contracting Committing in enforceable form 5 Ordering Deciding whose trade goes when 6 Settlement The only link where value moves 7 Enforcement Making the outcome stick Exactly one of those stages – settlement – happens on a blockchain, although it has seen outsized development efforts among those working on private finance infrastructure. As a result, the industry as a whole has made great strides in strengthening privacy in the settlement stage through work on blockchain architecture.  The other six stages often rely on systems owned by other people or third parties, and each of them contains multiple vectors for information leakage. Discovery can begin in a browser, which can expose your IP address, location, internet provider, and more. Connecting a wallet to a browser frontend links your onchain identity with that of your browser and device. In the diligence stage, looking up address data through hosted RPC providers leaves a trace back to you, allowing that provider to collect data and create and sell identity graphs. Read this interactive article about how your browser is betraying you for an idea of how your transaction can be compromised before it is even created. Negotiation is often done through hosted platforms or third-party services like Telegram or public mempools, where a record of your coordination is kept, and your identity is linked to other information exposed during the lifecycle. How Logos is patching the holes in coordination The coordination of a transaction has to happen somewhere, and a messaging layer is the natural place to begin. Logos Messaging comprises two modules for peer-to-peer communication: Chat and Delivery. Chat runs on top of Delivery, which can leverage the Mix protocol for improved privacy. Chat is the end-to-end encrypted user-facing application, while Delivery is the secure transport layer for peer-to-peer messaging. These modules inherit the underlying privacy-preserving communications infrastructure of the Logos stack, which includes a decentralised system that allows node operators to trustlessly peer with others who offer the services they need, without relying on a single source of truth. Read the full specification for more about decentralised peer discovery. When it comes to preserving privacy for transaction discovery, diligence, and negotiation, the Mix protocol aims to do a lot of heavy lifting. Designed as a decentralised, private routing layer for libp2p networks, it routes each packet through a decentralised overlay network composed of participating libp2p nodes, known as mix nodes. Read the full specification for more information about Mix . Peer-to-peer messaging protocols are often subject to spam or denial-of-service attacks, which Logos defends against through the implementation of  Rate Limiting Nullifier (RLN) that limits messages while preserving privacy. In addition to the above protocols that are part of the Logos stack’s privacy-preserving messaging capabilities, the infrastructure is also designed to be run locally, not accessed through a hosted provider. Basecamp is a desktop application that runs the Logos stack on your own machine. It is a return to local-first principles: the whole stack, node included, on hardware you control, installed the way any other application is installed, but without needing to trust a third party. It is an open and accessible interface for people who use Logos and the applications built on top of the stack, including private p2p chat, atomic swaps, or a blockchain wallet. Download and install Basecamp .  What’s being built in Logos Testnet v0.3 Much of what is currently being developed on the Logos stack is foundational infrastructure for reducing exposure across the transaction lifecycle. The first step in securing information along the design of PriFi is to reduce reliance on centralised operators and trusted third parties.  Trustless, verifiable protocols offer the decentralisation required for building truly private infrastructure, and version 3.0 of the Logos Testnet is deploying these protocols for early testing and integration by developers. Several protocol improvements in Testnet v0.3, which is expected to be released at the end of September, relate to coordination leaks in the transaction lifecycle. Service Discovery In Testnet v0.3, Service Discovery is available as a separate Logos Core module, configurable as an alternative to discv5 for ambient peer discovery, so that a node can ask for peers offering a specific capability without having to span several separate networks in order to find them.  The benchmark targets are comparable performance to discv5 when every node supports the same service and better performance when the service being sought is sparse, and the module API improves so that several modules can share a single Service Discovery instance instead of each running its own. Mix Testnet v0.3 sees substantial progress made on the development of the Mix protocol in Logos. It will be integrated into the Logos Delivery module with exposure on the Messaging API, and Mix nodes now have a local reputation record for peers. A new dedicated Mix module also allows Logos node operators to run Mix nodes via their Logos nodes. Large messages get an application-level mechanism that segments them and routes the pieces over multiple paths, with multiple-SURB paths for large responses.  Hidden services are specified and implemented so that providers can anonymously register and clients can discover and anonymously access them. A standalone Logos Mix module, encapsulating nim-libp2p-mix together with RLN-based denial-of-service protection and cover traffic, is also now available to be integrated by developers looking to experiment with building on Logos. RLN The simple method of preventing abuse of a p2p system is to know who people are and rate-limit per account, but this exposes who talks to a network and how often, removing any privacy gained by the p2p architecture. Rate-Limiting Nullifiers charge the sender a proof instead, so that a sender demonstrates they are within their allowance without revealing which member they are. If they exceed their allowance, they are exposed. Testnet v0.3 specifies and implements a basic RLN membership management module, migrates Logos Delivery onto LEZ-based RLN through it, and adds both a standalone membership allocation service and a full RLN module that generalises the mechanism so it can rate-limit anything on the stack, with advanced authentication techniques for membership allocation still under active research. Chat The Chat module is a user-facing chat application that bundles RLN, Scalable Data Sync, mix and de-MLS together, which allows a negotiation to be encrypted, reliably ordered, resistant to traffic analysis and protected from spam at the same time, with no central delivery service. Testnet v0.3 includes an early implementation of the λAccount mechanism, long-lived addresses that survive key rotation, which can be used to enable privacy-preserving diligence while requiring no third-party authorisation. The development of architecture for PriFi is an ongoing effort, which requires the rollout of foundationally privacy-preserving infrastructure to underpin truly private transactions across the lifecycle. In Testnet v0.3, this foundational architecture continues to be built out and will be available to developers to tinker with and contribute towards. Read more about the architecture of the Logos stack . Improvements coming to Basecamp Basecamp is the local-first launcher for privacy-preserving infrastructure.  Local-first means your node, your keys, and your data live on hardware you control, improving privacy within the discovery and diligence phases of the transaction lifecycle. A message or transaction sent from Basecamp enters the peer-to-peer network from your own machine, as a peer. Other nodes relay the traffic, and on testnet, the first hop is to bootstrap the infrastructure that the project runs. Basecamp is still in development, and v0.3 will continue to build out the open-source application, which is a gateway to any public applications compatible with the Logos stack. The app and many applications will receive an improved interface in Testnet v0.3, and Basecamp will continue to receive iterative updates aimed at improving its usability.  In addition, the package manager module can now be used to source module contents using CIDs via Logos Storage, reducing reliance on GitHub, although at this early stage of development, indexing and metadata will remain on GitHub. The place to build for PriFi The design philosophy of Logos, to build privacy-preserving infrastructure that unlocks parallel systems, makes it the best place to be for those interested in realising the vision of PriFi. Testnet v0.2.1 is running now. If you would like to get involved,  download Basecamp and run a node on your machine. If you want to contribute capacity and play a role in the network,  check out the node operator guide . Building infrastructure for everyone is an open, collaborative effort. If you have ideas, objections, or want to understand more about what Logos is building at the edge of PriFi,  join the conversation on the Logos forum . Build the parallel.

documents.title: PriFi and the Incomplete Institution: Securing the Transaction Supply Chain
documents.description: Extending imperative credibility beyond transaction settlement to reduce risks and costs
documents.body: For most of crypto’s history, we have treated onchain transactions as if they were atomic events. We tend to consider them as self-contained moments: a signed instruction enters the network, executes, and settles. In reality, they comprise a series of links in a wider chain. They include discovery, diligence, negotiation, contracting, ordering, settlement, and enforcement. Settlement is where blockchains are extraordinary. Bitcoin demonstrated that monetary rules could be enforced without reliance on a central operator who can make exceptions. Ethereum extended the principle to programmable agreements. A valid state transition is accepted; an invalid one is rejected. Counterparties do not need to trust a minister, bank manager, or platform operator to consistently honour rules. Institutions have always struggled with the problem of credible commitment: How can we trust that a party will act in accordance with agreements made when breaking their word may be in their interest? Blockchains realised historically unprecedented guarantees by removing the discretion to defect and making rules self-enforcing. Yet the absolute transparency that enables blockchain to structurally constrain defection introduces new attack surfaces by making information about the transaction available to every network observer. These attack surfaces discourage wider participation in onchain finance and define the problem space for those building PriFi infrastructure.  The proposition is not simply that financial transactions should be “more private”. It is that the correct unit of analysis is the entire transaction lifecycle, and that strengthening commitments requires heightened privacy and security at each link. The transaction lifecycle Ronald Coase observed that exchange itself is costly. Finding somebody to trade with, discovering prices, negotiating an agreement, and ensuring the other party holds up their end of the deal all require effort and therefore involve costs (Coase, 1937). Carl Dahlman later grouped these costs into three broad categories: search and information costs, bargaining and decision costs, and policing and enforcement costs (Dahlman, 1979). Building on Dahlman’s ideas, we can consider the transaction having a seven-step lifecycle: Discovery: finding a potential counterparty. Diligence: establishing who they are and whether their claims are credible. Negotiation: reaching an agreement on terms. Contracting: fixing those terms in a form intended to bind the parties. Ordering: determining the order in which transactions are processed. Settlement: the only link where value actually moves. Enforcement: making the agreed outcome stick after settlement. Settlement is the hinge. Everything before it prepares the parties to transfer value; everything after it makes the transfer durable. Consider a house purchase. The payment at completion may settle in a few minutes, but the economically meaningful transaction has already spent weeks passing through estate agents, inspections, searches, mortgage underwriting, price negotiations, contracting, and title verification. Securing the final bank transfer while leaving the previous stages open to fraud or manipulation would not secure the purchase in a way that would satisfy the counterparties to the deal. Similarly, if an institutional investor wants to build a large position, but their intentions leak during discovery or negotiation, other market participants can take advantageous positions that could compromise the profitability of the investor’s planned trade well before settlement occurs. Clearly, the security of a transaction cannot be judged by settlement alone. At every stage, somebody is entrusted with information, discretion, or control that could be exploited. Securing the transaction, therefore, requires more than protecting the movement of value: it requires safeguards at each of the seven links. That raises the question: What makes safeguards credible in the first place? What makes a commitment credible? Governments, banks, courts, companies, and protocols make promises about their future conduct. A government promises not to confiscate property. A central bank promises to protect the integrity of money. A regular bank promises to return deposits. An exchange promises to follow its stated rules. A platform promises not to misuse privileged information. The quality of those promises cannot be judged when keeping them is convenient. The real test is when defection becomes the more attractive option. Barry Weingast captured the political version of this commitment problem succinctly: a government strong enough to protect property is also strong enough to confiscate wealth (Weingast, 1995). The power that makes an institution useful can also make it a threat. The history of institutional development can, in part, be read as a history of attempts to manage that dilemma. Douglass North and Barry Weingast’s study of England after the Glorious Revolution argued that institutional changes, including greater parliamentary control over public finances, constrained the Crown’s ability to interfere arbitrarily with property and public credit. Over the following decades, government borrowing costs fell from 14% to around 3% as lenders became more confident that repayment was no longer simply a matter of royal discretion  (North & Weingast, 1989). We can broadly consider the quality of institutional commitments through two lenses: motivational credibility and imperative credibility. In the former case, the promiser can defect on a commitment but has a reason not to. This might be upholding their reputation, protecting pledged collateral, or securing repeat business.  Oliver Williamson’s work on private ordering and credible commitments describes arrangements designed to make opportunistic defection costly enough that continued cooperation becomes preferable (Williamson, 1983). Much of commercial society depends upon this form of credibility. However, its effectiveness depends on the incentives that sustain it. Imperative credibility is much stronger. Here, the discretion to defect has been removed structurally or made prohibitively expensive to exercise. The promise does not depend only on the operator choosing to uphold their side; some structural mechanism constrains their ability to renege on a deal. This is where cryptonetworks made their historic contribution.  A Bitcoin node does not reject an invalid block because protecting Bitcoin’s reputation seems commercially attractive. It rejects the block because the rules determining validity are constitutive of the system. The promise has migrated from institutional behaviour into institutional structure. Motivation and imperative commitments respond differently to pressure. Motivational credibility must be sustained by incentives. If those incentives change, the behaviour they support may also change. Imperative credibility instead narrows the space in which discretion can be exercised at all. This is the institutional breakthrough that cryptonetworks introduced. However, it only protects one link in the transaction lifecycle – settlement – while the absolute transparency required to achieve this unprecedented level of imperative credibility exposes other links to attacks. Two different hazards Classical transaction-cost economics is deeply concerned with opportunism. Williamson describes opportunism as “self-interest seeking with guile”: a counterparty may misrepresent what they are selling, withhold information, default after receiving payment, exploit an incomplete contract, or take advantage of a dependency that emerges after the other party has committed resources. These are hazards inside the transaction, and modern economies have developed an enormous institutional apparatus to manage them, including contracts, courts, escrow services, collateral, warranties, reputation, fiduciary duties, auditing, and, more recently, smart contracts.  However, there is another class of hazards in which an attacker may have no part in the transaction at all. These out-of-transaction hazards include thieves with knowledge of where assets are custodied, competitors taking advantage of known terms, extortionists who know what you can afford to pay, and searchers looking for onchain transactions to frontrun.  Each of the two hazard classes operates differently, and therefore, the defences against them are different. An opportunistic counterparty already has access to certain information. Dealing with somebody necessarily involves revealing things like who you are and what you hold. Therefore, protection must rely heavily on binding the counterparty’s behaviour through contracts, collateral requirements, possible reputational damage, or penalties for not upholding their end of the bargain. Those outside a deal usually do not have any relationship to the parties of the deal. Therefore, information becomes an essential first input. A burglar cannot target a safe whose existence is unknown. Nor can a rival bidder undercut a confidential offer it has never seen. Onchain, a searcher cannot frontrun an order it is unaware of. While information is not sufficient for predation on its own because an attacker still needs the capacity to act, it often determines whether there is a target in the first place. Blockchain strengthens settlement but reverses the informational default Classical transaction-level theory pays relatively little attention to this second class of hazard because commercial confidentiality was, to a significant extent, part of the institutional background in which exchange took place. A merchant kept their ledger private, banks developed duties of confidence, lawyers protected privileged communications, companies negotiated acquisitions behind closed doors, governments used sealed bids, and financial markets developed mechanisms for concealing large orders. These arrangements were imperfect, and information could still leak, but universal publication was not the default. Williamson distinguished between the “institutional environment” – the rules of the game – and the institutions of governance operating within that environment. Features of the environment could therefore be treated as background conditions while different governance structures were compared (Williamson, 1991). Confidentiality was, to a large extent, one of those background conditions. Transparent blockchains invert that condition. Information that was once fragmented across private ledgers, institutions, and counterparties is instead recorded in a common, persistent, and widely observable data structure. The cost of acquiring information, therefore, falls dramatically: what might require access to a bank, broker, counterparty, or court order outside of crypto becomes a database query. This changes the economics of the threat itself. An outsider who previously had to put effort into discovering that a transaction, asset, or position existed may now query information as a byproduct of the system’s operation. A hazard that could previously be mitigated as part of the institutional background moves into the transaction itself. Blockchain achieves unprecedented verifiability by making everything transparent by default. However, the same transparency that allows an honest observer to verify the system can also supply an unbound outsider with the information needed to identify, monitor, and potentially exploit a target. Security and privacy are complements With the two hazard classes identified, we can consider different approaches to protecting against them. The first is to bind or deter the actor who might harm you. Contracts, collateral, legal penalties, access controls, signature requirements, and consensus rules all fit this family. For this article, we will call this “security”. The second is to deny would-be attackers the information that makes targeting possible. For this article, we will call this “privacy”. These protections do not map perfectly onto the two hazard classes, but there is a strong asymmetry. You normally cannot starve a counterparty of all information. If somebody is lending against your assets, acquiring your company, or entering into a bilateral trade with you, they need to know something about you and your ability to honour the deal. The answer is selective disclosure plus binding. Outsiders present almost the reverse problem. They have signed nothing. They may live beyond your jurisdiction. They may never reveal their intentions unless they attack. You cannot negotiate confidentiality agreements with every thief, frontrunner, hostile competitor, data broker, or coercive authority that might eventually take an interest in your transaction. Therefore, when binding them becomes unfeasible, the efficient defence is to avoid sharing exploitable information with them. The two protections are complementary. Privacy without security is fragile. Revealing everything privately to an intermediary that remains free to betray you simply concentrates the attack surface. Security without privacy is incomplete. Perfectly protecting an asset while broadcasting a detailed targeting map tells every unbound outsider where to concentrate their attention. This insight has implications for property itself. An important strand of property theory treats the right to exclude as central to ownership (Honoré, 1961; Merrill, 1998). If information is an input into appropriation, it follows that controlling access to information about an asset may form part of the practical ability to exclude others from exploiting it. Mayshar, Moav, and Neeman make a related argument in political economy: the transparency of productive activity affects the ease with which its returns can be appropriated, and, in turn, the institutions that emerge around it (Mayshar, Moav, & Neeman, 2017). PriFi takes that intuition and applies it to the transaction level. A property right can be extraordinarily secure in the narrow sense that nobody can alter the ledger without authorisation, while remaining unusually weak in the informational sense that every potential claimant can observe the asset and its history. The result is a peculiar institutional object: a vault with exceptionally strong locks and perfectly transparent glass walls. Blockchain and the glass-vault problem Transparent blockchains create a genuine institutional inversion. At the rule layer, they are exceptionally strong. At the information layer, they are exceptionally legible. These two properties arise from the same architecture. Broadcasting everything to every participant made verification possible without relying upon a privileged insider. Anyone could reproduce the state transition and confirm that the rules had been followed. While that is a major achievement without historical parallel, a broadcast cannot distinguish between audiences. The same information reaches the counterparty, the verifier, the competitor, the thief, the analytics company, the searcher, and the state. Persistent ledgers compound the problem. Pseudonymity may protect an identity for some period, but identity and addresses can later be connected through an exchange, a payment for a physical good, an operational error, a public disclosure, or another external dataset. Once a connection is established, information recorded years earlier can acquire new meaning retrospectively. Furthermore, some attacks do not need the connection at all. For address poisoning, an onchain address is itself enough of a target. For many forms of maximal extractable value, transaction intention is the crucial input. For such strategies, the economically relevant fact may simply be that a sufficiently large position is visible and approaching a threshold. The human name behind the transaction may be irrelevant. This is why the transparency question cannot be reduced to anonymous addresses alone. When the chain works perfectly, but an attack is still successful The 2025 Bybit theft of $1.5 billion provides a clear illustration of transaction lifecycles extending far beyond settlement. The attack occurred around the signing process. The interface through which authorised participants understood the transaction they were approving was compromised. Once the signed instruction entered the mempool, the chain executed it. The settlement mechanism was not cryptographically defeated.  The uncomfortable lesson is that the blockchain could work exactly as intended, while the economic transaction still failed catastrophically. The settlement layer enforced what had been signed, not what was intended. The sixth link held, but the exploit had already occurred by that point. Privacy must not be patched in The obvious response is to make individual blockchain functions private. While that work is essential, the transaction-supply-chain framing leads to a more demanding conclusion: protection has a weakest-link structure. If the settlement is private but discovery reveals counterparties, an attacker moves to discovery. If balances are private but intentions enter a public queue before execution, an attacker moves to ordering. The vulnerability has been relocated, and so will the attack. Something similar happens when privacy is provided by a trusted intermediary. A private order-flow service can shield an order from the public mempool. That may materially improve the user’s position. However, the service itself acquires privileged information. The user has, therefore, exchanged public exposure for reliance upon a named intermediary.  The protection has migrated from imperative credibility back towards motivational credibility. The intermediary could misuse the information, but promises not to. That may be acceptable, and sometimes motivational commitments are entirely appropriate. However, a privacy mechanism that relocates discretion has moved, not eliminated, the commitment problem. As such, “PriFi” cannot simply mean “a private ledger”. It requires codesigning protection, considering both privacy and security, across the lifecycle under a common threat model. Checkability and readability are not the same There is an important objection to this argument: information can improve markets. George Stigler and Richard Posner both emphasised the economic costs of privacy, where it allows parties to conceal information relevant to a counterparty’s assessment or pricing of a transaction (Stigler, 1980; Posner, 1981). A borrower concealing insolvency from a lender is not creating a better market, and a seller concealing a defect from a buyer is not exercising economically productive privacy. The objection is real but applies most directly to the relationship between transacting parties. While a lender may need to know that a borrower satisfies a collateral requirement, it does not follow that every observer needs the borrower’s entire financial history. Similarly, a counterparty may need assurance that an offer is valid but would not appreciate competing bidders being able to see the bid ahead of an auction’s close.  The objective is, therefore, appropriate information revelation, not absolute secrecy. The distinction is between information disclosed because a particular relationship requires it and information disclosed merely because the infrastructure broadcasts it.  Modern cryptography makes this distinction increasingly actionable. Zero-knowledge proofs, selective disclosure systems, commitments, secure computation, and related techniques open a design space between the two extremes of “just trust me” and “show everyone everything”. For PriFi, the institutional objective should be to preserve auditability without requiring universal readability . PriFi as a research problem Under this framing, private finance is a problem of institutional completeness, rather than simply a niche for users with unusually strong preferences about privacy. Crypto has already demonstrated that architecture can remove discretion from one crucial part of exchange. PriFi asks what follows if we apply the same protections to the rest of the transaction.  How should counterparties discover one another without unnecessarily broadcasting their intentions? How can counterparties get the information necessary for exchange without creating permanent public dossiers? How should negotiation occur when metadata may reveal economic strategy? How should the operators who maintain network order be protected against coercion when identifying them is itself part of the attack? And so on. These questions sit across economics, distributed systems, cryptography, networking, mechanism design, information security, and institutional theory. PriFi: Protecting the entire transaction lifecycle Transactions pass through seven links. Every link creates positions from which somebody may be able to exploit the transaction. Those threats can be categorised into two different classes: opportunism among the parties and predation from outside them.  Each class requires a different form of protection. While security binds, constrains, and deters, privacy reduces unnecessary knowledge and, therefore, reduces the surface available for targeting. Neither protection substitutes completely for the other because a transaction inherits the weakness of the least protected link in the supply chain. Blockchains represent a remarkable institutional achievement because they supply imperative credibility at settlement. But the radical transparency required to achieve this introduces new vulnerabilities at other links in the chain.  PriFi involves bringing the same level of credibility to each link in the chain. It is not privacy bolted onto existing systems but rather systems designed from the ground up to allow counterparties to conceal valuable and exploitable information such that they can confidently enter into trades. Build PriFi infrastructure on Logos Basecamp .  Explore sample PriFi tools on Logos .  Learn more about how Logos secures the complete transaction supply chain.   This article is based on research compiled by Logos cofounder Jarrad Hope and ideas emerging from it. PriFi is central to Logos’ goal to revitalise civil society. Effective parallel organising requires economic rails that can withstand outside efforts to obstruct and manipulate activity. documents.title: Field Station / Rajasthan: A Coliving Residency to Build the Parallel
documents.description: A parallel society experiment with Zu-Grama
documents.body: Field Station is deliberately different from a conventional hackathon. There is no conference centre to arrive at in the morning and leave at the end of the day. Residents will live, share meals, and build together on a 500-acre regenerative living project, working alongside people from different disciplines and testing what they create against real local problems. Applications are now open. More than a hack space Most hackathons compress collaboration into a weekend. Participants form a team, build quickly, present something, and then go home. Field Station explores what happens when people spend longer together and share more than a workspace. Residents will cohabit the site, with accommodation and meals provided. Days will combine focused build time with workshops, mentoring, and stand-ups. Outside those sessions, life at Dhun becomes part of the programme too: shared farm-to-table meals, walks, foraging, field lunches, and phone-free communal evenings. That is intentional. Building resilient communities is not only a technical problem. It also depends on trust, cooperation, and the everyday habits that allow groups of people to coordinate efficiently. Field Station creates space to experiment with both at once. Instead of talking abstractly about new forms of social organisation, residents will spend eight days living them. Proof, not hype The same principle applies to what gets built. Field Station is centred on working solutions rather than speculative pitches. Builders are encouraged to arrive with something concrete, such as an existing project, prototype, experiment, or clearly scoped problem, and spend their time at the residency tailoring it to solve a previously identified, real issue affecting the communities surrounding the event’s site. One of the residency’s civic challenges, for example, asks builders to explore better ways of reporting and responding to everyday local issues: water, waste, access, maintenance, and other problems that need to move visibly from “reported” to “in progress” to “resolved”. Another focuses on privacy-preserving mutual aid: tools that can help residents and site staff coordinate things they actually need, from transport and supply runs to skills and practical help. These are deliberately ordinary problems. Infrastructure only matters when somebody actually uses it. A coordination tool becomes interesting when people coordinate with it. A reporting system proves itself when somebody reports a real problem, and someone else acts on it.  At Field Station, the environment is not just a backdrop for building. It directly informs what gets built. Four ways to take part Residents can apply through four tracks. Logos Civic Prize Track Builders in the Civic Prize Track will work on specific, live problems identified through Logos Circles and adapted to the local setting. The initial challenges focus on civic reporting, community response, and privacy-preserving mutual-aid coordination. Teams will be able to use the Logos stack to create tools that can be piloted during the residency rather than disappearing after demo day. Logos Sovereignty and Privacy Track This track is for people already building tools, applications, and protocols that put greater control over data and infrastructure into their users' hands. Participants can bring an existing work in progress or a well-scoped idea and develop it using Logos's private-by-default infrastructure. Projects might address the needs of Dhun, Jaipur, a participant's own community, or the wider Logos network. The important part is having a credible path from idea to something people can run, test, and use. Zu-Grama d/acc Track Led by Zu-Grama, the d/acc track looks more broadly at technologies designed to preserve and strengthen human agency as AI and digital systems become more powerful. Areas of interest include AI alignment and safety, AI for science, neurotechnology, biotech, collective intelligence, sense-making, civic technology, cryptography, governance, and other forms of d/acc-aligned infrastructure. The track is intended for people with a serious question, project, or experiment that can move materially forward during the residency, particularly where collaboration across disciplines can produce something that would be difficult to achieve alone. Resident, Non-Builder Track Not everyone at Field Station writes code. Activists, community organisers, artists, writers, testers, and explorers are also invited to apply. Their role is not peripheral to the experiment: technology that is meant to serve communities needs people ready to use it, challenge it, document it, and decide whether it is actually useful. Non-builder residents will help dogfood projects, provide feedback, and participate in judging submissions. Artists and writers will also help bring a cultural element to the week, further distinguishing it from conventional hackathons that often consist entirely of whiteboards and terminals. Why Dhun? Field Station takes place in Dhun, Rajasthan, on a 500-acre regenerative living project, around 60–90 minutes from Jaipur International Airport. The setting is deliberately removed from the usual conference or coworking environment. Residents will share accommodation; eat dishes prepared with locally available crops, grains, and nuts; and spend their evenings together rather than dispersing back to hotels. There will still be plenty of time to develop projects. The daily rhythm includes stand-ups, mentoring, workshops, and more than four hours of uninterrupted build time. But the spaces between those sessions matter, too. A conversation over lunch can change the direction of a project. Someone testing a tool over dinner can expose an assumption its builders missed. A problem noticed on the farm in the morning can become something a team starts solving that afternoon. That continuity is one of the central experiments behind Field Station. Build the parallel then test, use, and improve The residency will culminate in a summit and demo night where participants show what they have built, what happened when people used it, and their next steps. Strong projects from the Logos tracks will also have the opportunity to unlock milestone-based grant funding to continue development. But the goal is to test a different model for living and creating together.  Field Station brings technologists together with activists, artists, organisers, researchers, and users. Converging in an environment where problems are tangible, they’ll eat together, test things, break them, fix them, iterate based on how real people use them, and leave with more than a slide deck. Field Station / Rajasthan runs from 23–31 October 2026 at Dhun, Rajasthan. Applications are open from 11–26 September. Around 30 residents will be selected across the four tracks. Apply now to Field Station / Rajasthan to build the parallel with Logos and Zu-Grama.

documents.title: Logos Dev Update: August 2026
documents.description: Your monthly update on the development of the Logos technology stack.
documents.body: Logos provides monthly updates on the state of the technology stack and the development of its various modules, giving developers a clear snapshot of development highlights from the past month.  August's work centred on the consensus layer of the Logos Blockchain, with uncle references and compressed block proposals both landing, alongside a finalised specification for the Logos Oracle Zone and a full redesign of the library delivering spam resistance across the stack. These updates further enhance the integrability and privacy-preserving capabilities of modules while hardening the overall stack. The updates listed here are some of the most important highlights from the past month. Work progresses on many facets of the stack simultaneously, and a more complete, technical breakdown is available at  roadmap.logos.co . For developer-focused highlights on X, please follow  Logos Tech . For broader updates on the Logos movement as a whole, stay tuned to the main  Logos account. Uncle references in Cryptarchia Cryptarchia is the privacy-preserving leadership lottery of the Logos Blockchain, where singular stakes are never revealed. The total therefore has to be inferred from block production. Cryptarchia blocks now carry  uncle references , restoring discarded evidence and keeping Total Stake Inference accurate as delay rises.  The  Total Stake Inference report sets out the method in full.. Compressed block proposals Compressed block proposals are now working end to end, including support in Blend. Proposals reference their transactions by a short prefix rather than a full hash, with the serialisation aligned between the implementation and the specification. Proposal size falls by roughly half as a result, and because every proposal travels over Blend, that reduction reduces the bandwidth Blend requires of the nodes running the protocol. Channel participation in Proof-of-Stake The Logos Blockchain token does two jobs. It secures the network through Proof-of-Stake, and it bridges into zones so applications can use it. Once bridged, funds were unable to participate in consensus and shrank the stake securing the network. The Channel Participation in Proof-of-Stake  LIP removes that trade-off, allowing bridged funds become on-ledger channel notes and allowing channels to redistribute the rewards earned on bridged funds to their users. The Logos Oracle Zone specification The  Logos Oracle Zone specification is now finalised. The design is optimistic and stays lightweight for the Logos Execution Zone by outsourcing signature verification to the Logos Blockchain, with the execution zone checking signatures only when a price is disputed. Work on implementation continued alongside the specification, with the proposer selection mechanism merged, a first oracle register contract built, and the indexer now able to follow and compute an attested price per channel and feed. The de-MLS boundary contract A new research discussion was opened around the  de-MLS boundary contract . De-MLS runs a decentralised MLS conversation driven purely by the application that calls it. The central property is passivity. De-MLS performs no network operations, so it acts only when the application calls it, and every call hands back the time remaining until the next one is due. Storage, identity, and transport are operated by the application, while the group handle and every protocol decision belong to de-MLS. Zerokit v3.0.0 launched Zerokit is the Rust implementation of Rate Limiting Nullifier, the anonymous rate-limiting primitive that underpins spam resistance in Logos. The  latest version is a full redesign of its internals, public API, and FFI and WASM boundaries. The headline change moves mode selection from a compile-time feature to runtime and type-level configuration, so behaviour is chosen when the library is used rather than fixed when it is built. State is now a type-state on RLN, the tree backend is now a type parameter, and message-id mode is now a runtime enum. Logos Delivery module update A  new version of the Logos Delivery module is live and fully backwards compatible, so existing integrations need no changes to integrate the latest version. It brings a newly bundled logos-delivery, tighter handling of calls, and Store and Postgres fixes addressing partition bloat and leaks. The Messaging API itself is unchanged in this release. A tutorial for the Storage API A  new tutorial was published in the Logos documentation. It covers building a Logos Core module that wraps the asynchronous Storage API in a synchronous command-line tool, then publishing a file and downloading it back by content identifier. The tutorial joins the wider body of storage documentation recently migrated onto  docs.logos.co , and is accurate for Testnet v0.2.1. Logos Broadcast Network and Circles Throughout August, Logos contributors continued to host online and IRL Circles around the world, creating digital and physical space to solve real-world problems with privacy-preserving technology. The Logos Broadcast Network continued to deliver regular programming, from Dev Club sessions and weekly technical updates to office hours every Friday at 14:00 UTC. Join these office hours to learn more about building on the Logos stack or to get help with specific issues. Full schedules and participation details are available at  press.logos.co/calendar and  logos.co/circles . For a full list of upcoming Logos events, check out the event page on  Luma . To get the latest developer updates from the Logos stack, follow  Logos Tech on X. Stay tuned to the main  Logos account for news on the wider global movement.

documents.title: State of the Logos Network: August 2026
documents.description: Your roundup of recent developments from the Logos social movement and tech stack
documents.body: Museum of Civil Liberties opens In August, Past.Present.Future., a new initiative exploring the systems that shape our freedoms and the forces that continue to erode them, went live. It begins with The Past and a trip to the Museum of Civil Liberties, an online museum tracing pivotal moments when our agency over money, communication, and political expression was weakened. The museum is a reminder of why privacy-preserving, censorship-resistant technologies are at the heart of Logos. Enter the museum to explore the events that brought us here, from the end of the gold standard and the expansion of post-9/11 surveillance to internet shutdowns and the weaponisation of personal data.  The Past is only the beginning: The Present and The Future are coming soon, extending the story of our eroding freedoms and where we’re heading if we don’t change course.  Enter the Museum of Civil Liberties. Raising chat control awareness  Last month, Logos launched a new initiative examining the EU and UK’s latest efforts to regulate online safety through private-message scanning and age verification. Both are presented as targeted measures to protect children, but in practice they require much broader systems for inspecting communications or verifying the identities of ordinary users. The initiative presents peer-reviewed research, large-scale empirical studies, and evidence from leading cryptographers and security researchers to show why these measures will fail at their stated goals while imposing significant threats to privacy and freedom. This is a core reason Logos exists: to build privacy-preserving, censorship-resistant technologies that uphold freedoms structurally rather than waiting for policy promises that rarely result in lasting change. Check out the chat control initiative homepage. If you’re local, join Logos Circle / London to support. Muster on Logos: Showing privacy leaks across the transaction lifecycle This month, Corey shared Muster, a sample application built on Logos to explore what privacy looks like across the full lifecycle of a transaction, not just at the point where value moves onchain. The demo brings encrypted messaging, coordination, negotiation, and private settlement into a single workflow, while also surfacing where information is exposed along the way. Muster provides a useful demonstration of the PriFi thesis: protecting a transaction at settlement is not enough if intent, counterparties, terms, or identity leak through the tools used before and after it. By keeping more of that activity within the same privacy-oriented infrastructure, Logos can reduce dependence on fragmented, centrally operated services, and give users greater visibility and control over what they reveal.  Learn more and  experiment with Muster . Parallel Dispatch launches Parallel Dispatch is a new biweekly newsletter that highlights developments threatening our freedoms and the tech and people defending them. Expect a curated selection of topical stories covering legal updates, activist movements, and resistance technologies from around the world. Sign up at the bottom of the  Logos homepage .  Parallel Dispatch also features bite-sized interviews with pioneers building, theorising, or taking action to support the parallel society movement. The first was with Ann Brody, an interdisciplinary researcher and digital rights advocate whose work explores how decentralised technologies shape governance and collective organising. IRL / Upcoming Over the coming months, Logos is exploring plans for a linked series of residencies, technical gatherings, and cultural activations focused on privacy, coordination, and developing real world solutions on sovereign infrastructure. Potential activities include hands-on experimentation with the Logos stack, community-led organising, and collaborations with artists and independent networks. Stay tuned for updates. More details will be shared as plans develop, IRL / August Zanzalu Over three weeks at Zanzalu, the Logos community put both its technology and its approach to grassroots organising into practice. Participants explored Basecamp, learned how to get Logos nodes online, joined permaculture training, and connected with local projects to share skills and learn from existing community initiatives. A highlight was returning to Straight Training Center, a community-run school supporting more than 120 students in Zanzibar. Last year,  Logos Circle / Zanzibar helped raise funds for 10 Raspberry Pis to equip its computer room. This year, the team saw those computers in use, delivered children’s books collected through Logos Circle / Lisbon, ran English reading and conversation classes, and took part in music and cultural exchange sessions with students. The visit also helped lay the groundwork for what comes next. Footage was captured for a short film to support future fundraising, while the Zanzibar Circle began looking at how it can help the school achieve its next major goal: constructing a permanent base to give the centre greater stability and room to expand.  Learn more . Logos Circles / August Highlights Logos Circles are open, locally led groups where people come together to turn shared concerns into practical action. Members identify issues that matter in their communities, build grassroots responses, and connect those efforts to the wider global network, using Logos technologies where they add value. More about Circles Find a Circle near you Propose a new  Circle In August, Circles formed in: / Awka / Lisbon / Kano / Zanzibar / Ede / Abeokuta / Khartoum / Abuja / Vizag / Calabar / Aba / Monrovia / Katsina / Kampala / Ibadan / Delta / Kaduna / Wukari / Yoal / Zaria / Sokoto / Gombe City / Bauchi / Maraba / Keffi / Benin / Minna / Ilorin /  Check the Logos Forum for individual progress updates on each Circle’s winnable issues. Logos Circle / Wukari supports local orphanage On 29 August, Logos Circle / Wukari held its first community outreach at Success Orphanage Home in Pwadzu. Sixteen members took part, bringing food, hygiene supplies, mosquito nets, and donated clothing, while also meeting with the orphanage matron to better understand the home’s most urgent needs. The Circle identified major challenges around clean water, overcrowding, and access to education, and arranged two volunteer maths and English tutors. The group is now planning a follow-up focused on beds and mattresses, water access, medical screenings, and additional hygiene support.  Learn more . Logos Circles / September Logos Circles are already planned in the cities below in September: / Portharcourt (3 Sept):  Get involved. / Uyo (5 Sept):  Get involved .  / Awka (5 Sept):  Get involved . / Kano (5 Sept):  Get involved . Several Logos Circles are still putting the finishing touches to their September plans, so only a handful of gatherings are confirmed at the moment. Check the  Logos events calendar or the  Circles discussion channel later this month for the latest events near you. No Circle in your area yet?  Get involved and start one . Tech stack highlights In August, two new releases of  Logos Testnet v0.2 were shipped in quick succession, delivering iterative improvements.  Logos Storage also pushed an update that brings better NAT traversal to node operators, making it considerably easier to run a node from a home network. Two long-running pieces of work reached completion during the month.  Zerokit v3.0.0 was released, completing the rearchitecture of the zero-knowledge library that powers RLN across Logos and the Status app, and the Logos Oracle Zone specification was finalised. A faster network transport passed its scale testing, and message reliability went live in Status Communities, where messages that would previously have gone missing are now recovered automatically.  Logos Core also saw an important security change, moving privilege out of the Basecamp interface so that no part of what a user sees on screen holds system-level access by default. Research continued across network measurement, post-quantum readiness, and cross-zone coordination. Logos Media Blog The Logos Blog features ongoing technical updates, movement news, and longer-form thinking on parallel organising and the ideas behind it. If you have a topic or perspective you’d like to contribute,  send us a proposal . In August, we published:  Interzone Bridging: Moving Value Between Zones on Logos Running Logos Basecamp is Easy, as the HodlUp Podcast Found Out Parallel Education and Effective Community Action in Delhi Logos Broadcast Network Each month, the Logos Broadcast Network creates space for people across the movement to share ideas, knowledge, and perspectives. The schedule spans community sessions such as Logos Circle / Online, developer-focused technical streams, discussions on new models of coordination, and deep dives into the Logos stack and the technologies surrounding it. Check the Logos Broadcast Network calendar to see upcoming streams . Ideas / Parallel Lives August saw the first instalment of a new format on the Logos Broadcast Network. Parallel Lives invites those living outside the system to discuss their stories. It replaces our previous Thursday philosophical sessions three weeks out of every month. Then, on the last Thursday of each month, the Sovereignty Super Space welcomes Parallel Society coalition partners and other big names at the intersection of tech and activism to discuss approaches to parallel organising.  August streams included:  Surveillance as a Service (with Matt and Jason of Free Thought Project) Parallel Lives: RPGs, Nomadism, and Privacy (with Kenny Palurintano) Sovereignty Superspace (with Cake Wallet’s Seth, DarkFi’s Amir Taaki, and Nym’s Alexis Roussel) Follow  Logos on X or  YouTube to join these discussions every Thursday. Technical The Logos Broadcast Network also connects developers with the wider community through a regular programme of technical streams. In August, sessions included: Logos Dev Club (Lambda prize updates, Persona wallet, and chess on Logos Basecamp) Logos Dev Club (P2P apps built on Logos) Inside Logos Mixnet Logos Dev Club (multisig on Logos, Muster exposes privacy leaks, encrypt everything with Keycard) Proof of Work Onboarding and Decentralised Sequencing Follow  Logos Tech on X and subscribe to the  Logos YouTube channel to take part in all future technical explorations and demos. Office hours Logos Office Hours are weekly sessions designed to help the community better understand, use, and build with the Logos stack.  Join every Friday at 12:00 UTC to speak directly with Logos engineers, ask questions, and deepen your understanding of the technology stack. Logos Circle / Online Logos Circle / Online is a weekly space for people taking on real challenges in their local communities. Each session combines practical guidance on starting a Logos Circle with insights from participants who are already organising and putting ideas into practice. Logos Circle / Online is on Tuesdays; join us   via the  Logos X account or  Logos YouTube channel. Community champions Logos grows through the people who contribute to it. From developers and engineers to researchers, builders, and community leaders, every contribution helps advance the mission, strengthen the network, and turn shared ideas into meaningful action. These community champions went above and beyond in August:  ParadoxComputer for their continued work on  Zonescan , a block explorer for Logos Execution Zones. [NODERS] for their work on a block  explorer and faucet for the Logos testnet. Guru for shipping  Xenia , a serverless AI inference marketplace over Logos Messaging.  Bristin for their work  stress testing Logos Zones . Vladimir for connecting Alisher with Russian- and English-speaking communities to host  Logos node-running workshops . Austine for their inspiring  medical care fundraising initiative.  Amelia and Paschal for all their hard work in Zanzibar. All the stewards hosting Logos Circles in June, and everyone who attended. Anyone building on Logos tech. Everyone who joined a Logos Broadcast Network stream or read a Logos Blog article. Your work could be featured in an upcoming community spotlight. Technical and non-technical contributions are equally welcome, so share what you’re building, researching, organising, or improving on  the forum or  Discord .  Find a way to contribute, create something useful, and help move Logos forward. Build the parallel.   Logos builds technologies and a social movement to revitalise civil society. We need developers, designers, writers, and activists to help shape it. Come build the parallel with us. Build on Logos.  Write for Logos Blog. Join a Logos Circle.

documents.title: Parallel Education and Effective Community Action in Delhi
documents.description: Taking grassroots action to fill gaps in Delhi’s education system with Logos Circle / Delhi
documents.body: The most impactful community initiatives rarely start with endless planning behind closed doors. That’s what legacy institutions do, and if it were effective, we wouldn’t need Logos Circles. Instead, they start by getting out there, finding the people who need support and listening to the challenges they face. Logos Circles / Delhi did exactly that. Their work with a local volunteer-led education initiative is truly inspiring and should serve as a blueprint for others to follow. Their approach perfectly encapsulates  what Logos Circles are : self-organised local groups taking practical action on issues that matter to their communities. They don’t wait for permission to get stuck in. For Logos Circle / Delhi, that meant supporting a group of volunteers already teaching children at risk of falling through  gaps in the Indian capital’s education system , in the open air – literally under a tree – and asking what would help make their work more stable. The Circle began with a site visit: sitting in on classes, speaking with the volunteers and children, identifying challenges, and running a small drive for notebooks and learning materials. Going forward, Logos Circle / Delhi aims to help turn the informal tuition group into a stable community learning hub, with a reliable tutor roster, a fixed schedule, consistent supplies, basic learning-progress tracking, and eventually a space that can keep classes running through Delhi’s monsoon season. They quickly moved from identifying the problem to getting involved in an easy but high-impact way. The Circle didn’t take on something grandiose and try to build a solution from scratch. They found an existing community initiative and asked how they could help it survive and grow. The Circle is also  running a Logos node and beginning to explore where the Logos stack can strengthen the coordination layer around the project. Logos Circle / Delhi’s steward Devisha shared what they’ve learned about effective grassroots planning and how their approach can be replicated elsewhere. Community action and parallel organising with Logos Circle / Delhi Hey Devisha, thanks for taking the time to talk about the work Logos Circle / Delhi is involved with. Let’s dive right in. Hi. Yeah, let’s do it!   How did you discover the education initiative, and why did you pick it to focus the Delhi Circle’s energy on first? We found it through a friend, who saw that these classes were going on near society in an open ground, where a group of volunteers were already running open-air tuition classes for children in Delhi NCR, quite literally under a tree. No building, no funding, no institution behind them. Just people who decided these children shouldn't go untaught. We picked it because it was already alive. When our Circle sat down to choose a winnable issue, a lot of ideas on the table were things we'd have to build from zero; this one wasn't. The community had already responded to a failure of the formal system by organising its own answer. It just had no support structure to keep it standing. That felt like exactly the kind of thing a Circle should exist for. We're not there to arrive with a solution and tell a community what it needs. We're there to find something people are already doing against the odds and make it durable. It's also unambiguously winnable: we can't fix education in Delhi, but we can help one learning group go from fragile to stable, and we'll be able to point at the difference. Can you briefly describe the problems with education in and around Delhi? The headline numbers make Delhi look better than it is. Enrolment is high, and the secondary dropout rate is around 4.8%, which sounds manageable. But two things hide underneath that. First, being enrolled and being educated are not the same thing. India's larger learning crisis is well documented – large numbers of children sit in classrooms for years without reaching grade-level reading or arithmetic. Delhi has historically scored below the national average on learning outcomes, and it sits in the middle band on the government's own Performance Grading Index for 2025-26. The Delhi government itself has said it is working to identify around 750,000 students with learning gaps. That's an admission of scale from the system itself. Second, the children we work with often don't appear in the statistics at all. Migrant families, children of daily-wage workers, kids who dropped out between Class 5 and Class 6, children whose families move between cities and lose their school seat in the process.  There were roughly 30,000 students in one year alone who finished Class 5 and never entered Class 6. Those children don't show up as a dropout crisis in a dashboard. They just quietly disappear from the pipeline. There's also a capacity problem. Vacant principal and teacher posts in Delhi government schools have been flagged repeatedly. So, even the children inside the system are often in overcrowded classrooms with no individual attention. The gap isn't only access. It's attention.   Does the education initiative that the Circle is supporting target a specific student demographic?  Yes. For now, we're focused on students in grades 7 to 10, and that's a deliberate decision driven by what we can actually deliver well. Our volunteers currently have subject expertise in maths, English, and science at that level. We could have spread ourselves across every age group that turns up, but we'd have done it badly. Teaching a Class 9 student science and teaching a six-year-old to read are completely different skills, and pretending otherwise helps nobody. We'd rather do a narrow thing properly than a broad thing thinly. There's also a timing argument for this band. Grades 7 to 10 are where children are most at risk of falling away permanently; it's the stage where accumulated gaps become unmanageable, where the pressure to start earning kicks in, and where a child who's struggling decides school isn't for them. Catching someone at Class 8 who is two years behind is hard, but very doable.  This is a starting point, not a policy. As we onboard more volunteers with different subject strengths, particularly foundational literacy for the younger children, we'll widen the age range. The constraint is our capacity, not the need. The need is for every age.   Is the education based on a specific curriculum, or is it more general to allow disadvantaged children to catch up? It's a mix, and the balance shifts by student. Because we're working with grades 7 to 10, the NCERT/state board syllabus matters. These students are heading towards board exams, and teaching them something disconnected from what they'll be assessed on would be unfair to them. So, the subjects our volunteers teach – maths, English, science – track the standard curriculum for those grades. Sitting in on the classes, this was one of the things we specifically went to understand: what they teach, in what order, and where it breaks down. The honest answer is that the curriculum is currently held in the heads of the volunteers rather than written down anywhere. That's one of the gaps we want to help close: not to impose a syllabus from outside, but to help them document what they're already doing so it survives any individual volunteer leaving, and so progress can actually be measured. How was the Circle's help received by the organisers and children? It was our first session, so we just went, sat, listened, and asked questions about what are the gaps in their education. Five of our volunteers spent the day with around 65 children in genuinely brutal heat. We sat with them, went through what they were learning, and ran a small supplies drive: notebooks and basic materials. The organisers have been doing this without help for a long time. Our position from the first conversation was that they are the institution and we're there to make their work sustainable. Once that landed, the conversation became very practical very quickly: what they actually need, what breaks every month, what they've never had time to fix. The children showing up at all is the part I'd emphasise. Nobody makes them come. There's no register, no consequence for skipping. They walked through 40-plus degree heat because someone said there'd be a class. That tells you the demand isn't the problem.   Is Logos Circle / Delhi’s initiative reproducible by other Circles? How should Circle stewards go about doing so? Very reproducible, probably more than most Circle projects, because the pattern doesn't depend on anything specific to Delhi. Almost every city has a version of this: a community already running something the state should be running, held together by a handful of unpaid people. What I'd tell another steward: Look for what already exists before you invent anything. The instinct is to design a project. Walk your area and find the people already doing the work. Supporting an existing effort is faster, cheaper, and far more likely to survive than launching your own. First visit: Sit, watch, ask. You'll learn the real problems, which are almost never the ones you assumed. Talk to the organisers as partners. They've solved problems you haven't thought about yet. Ask what breaks: the answers are more useful. Choose a winnable version. Not “fix education”. Ours is: in six months, turn an informal tuition group into a stable learning hub with fixed schedule, tutor roster, progress tracking, reliable supplies. Small enough to actually finish. Fix consistency before you fix anything else. A predictable weekly slot is worth more than a large one-off donation. Most of these efforts don't die from lack of money; they die from irregularity. Document from day one. Baseline numbers, photos, notes.    What would make the biggest difference to the children’s education if it arrived tomorrow? Three things, in this order: Committed volunteer tutors. This is the binding constraint. Five volunteers for 30-45 children is not a ratio at which anyone learns to read. Ten reliable people who show up every week would transform outcomes more than any amount of equipment. And “committed” matters more than “qualified”. Consistency beats credentials with these children. A monsoon-proof space. Right now, the classroom is a tree. That works for part of the year, and then it doesn't. A shared room, a community hall, even a covered courtyard would take an entire category of disruption off the table. A recurring supplies pipeline instead of one-off drives. We did a notebook distribution and it was lovely, but it's not a system. A small, predictable monthly budget sponsored by a few people rather than donated in a burst would mean nobody has to teach without materials again.   Is there scope for Logos technologies to be incorporated into the initiative? Yes, but not with the children, as most of them don't have phones or computers; the beneficiaries are not online, but the technology serves the coordination layer around them. That layer is real, and it has real problems: Tutor and volunteer coordination.  A materials archive on Logos Storage.  Transparent community funding. For the supplies pipeline and eventually the learning space. We're watching what  Circle / Benin built with FundBrave, and  Circle / Abeokuta is using. Small-donor education funding in India has a real trust problem: people want to give but don't believe that the money actually arrives. Transparent, auditable allocation is a direct answer to that.   How did you find the Logos node setup process?  Honestly, it was more approachable than I expected. Running it through Basecamp meant I didn't have to touch a command line. It's a normal desktop install, and the node dashboard is built in. Also, thanks to Alisher for guiding me step by step on it.   The Indian government plans to upgrade many school libraries and classrooms this year. What do you think? Will it close the gap? Will initiatives like Logos Circle / Delhi’s still be needed? I think it's genuinely good news, and I don't want to be cynical about it. Delhi is upgrading 125 school libraries with digital devices and kiosks, and setting up thousands of smart classrooms. But it won't close the gap, for a simple structural reason: these upgrades reach children who are inside the system. The children we teach are outside it. A smart classroom does nothing for a child who isn't enrolled. A digital library doesn't help a girl who left after Class 5 when her family migrated, or a boy whose parents need him working by afternoon. Infrastructure improves the experience of the enrolled. It doesn't reach the ones who fell out. The children we work with don't primarily lack devices. They lack an adult with time who knows exactly where they're stuck. That's not something you can procure. So yes, initiatives like this will still be needed, and I'd argue the two aren't in competition. The ideal outcome isn't that we replace the state; it's that we catch the children the state's programmes structurally can't reach, and where possible get them back into the system, ready to actually use those new libraries. That's really what a parallel institution means to us. Not opposition, but coverage of the space the existing system doesn't reach.   Truly inspiring! Thanks for sharing your story, Devisha. Keep on doing amazing things. Thank you! And anytime. Inspired? Take action now Logos Circle / Delhi is a testament to the power of grassroots collective action. They saw a problem and got to work. That’s the whole point of Logos Circles. You can do the same in your local community.  Propose a new Circle , take the steward training, and start making a difference where you live.   Join a Circle .  Run Logos Basecamp .  Build the parallel.
