documents.title: Running Logos Basecamp is Easy, as the HodlUp Podcast Found Out
documents.description: Dr Corey Petty on how to run Basecamp and why Logos is going after full-stack privacy with zero compromises
documents.body: Long-time Logos evangelist Dr Corey Petty recently joined the HodlUp podcast to discuss privacy, parallel societies, AI, building better institutions, and where Logos is headed. While the whole podcast is well worth listening to, the main take-home message was just how simple it is to run the Logos stack on hardware you control via Logos Basecamp. Find out below. Basecamp is a fully local launcher for the complete Logos stack, running all default modules – Storage, Messaging, and Blockchain – along with installable modules and apps that expand its capabilities on a device you control.  Learn more about Logos Basecamp . Watch Corey on the HodlUp Podcast. Logos development progress  Logos Testnet v0.2.1 is live, and most of the core stack is functional, including execution environments and private atomic swaps. Development is beyond "wait for testnet launch" and into the "harden and grow" phase. And for that, the network needs real usage, not just sideline spectators.  Run Logos Testnet v0.2.1 now .  Explore the Logos stack's base of operations Running Basecamp to get started with Logos is easy: Just  download Basecamp and click run . That's the entire install. Basecamp requires minimal system specs: a Raspberry Pi is enough. It’s going to get even easier to run: more deployment options are on the way, so you won't need to dedicate your main machine to it. What can you do for Logos Basecamp? You can help harden the Logos stack. Get involved by: Trying to break it. Run a node, play around with it,  file any issues you encounter . Building on it. The stack is ready for you to use.  Get involved . Applying for a grant.   RFPs are open for contributions that expand Logos’ usability and functionality. Why building on Basecamp matters The more developers building on Basecamp and exploring its capabilities, the sooner we'll arrive at the mainnet release. Simply running a node through Basecamp increases the anonymity set for all users, and building novel modules for Basecamp can reveal bugs in the code that need to be addressed before the network goes fully live.  As Corey mentioned on the HodlUp Podcast, the bar for Logos’s success isn't a roadmap item shipping on time; it's someone building something the engineers behind it never anticipated. Logos is meant to be built collectively in the open, not developed behind closed doors.  Watch Corey on HodlUp Download Basecamp Explore developer grants and open RFPs Basecamp video tutorials If you’re not ready to dive in and explore Basecamp yourself yet, the video tutorials below show just how easy it is to get it up and running and start your journey. Quickstart Logos Basecamp Installing Logos Basecamp Understanding .lgx Modules on Logos Basecamp Building Your First “Hello-World” UI Module on Logos Basecamp If you’re struggling with anything Basecamp-related, you can put your questions to the engineers who built it during Logos Office Hours. They’re every Friday at 12:00 UTC.  Attend an office hour . You can also  ask for help at any time in the Logos Discord . What's already running on Basecamp Since the Logos Testnet v0.1’s release in March, developers have been busy building new modules and sample applications for it. The examples below may not have been updated to run on the latest version of Basecamp, but they do show what’s possible with the stack and will hopefully inspire the development of new modules. IA Archiver: Preserve Internet Archive items on Logos Storage.  Learn more . Anon Forum:  An old-school anonymous forum on local infra.  Learn more . Receiver:  A sovereign internet radio module.  Learn more . DOOM on Basecamp: Run the legendary shoot-em-up inside Basecamp.  Learn more .  We're building technologies and a social movement to revitalise civil society. We need developers, designers, writers, and activists to help shape it. Come build the parallel with us. Run Logos Basecamp. Read the docs. Join a Logos Circle. Transcript: Why Privacy Can’t Be Bolted On In Crypto Atis Shala: Hello Corey, how's it going? Corey Petty: Going well. Happy to be here, good to meet y'all. I was looking you guys up, doing some background research, and I think this is going to be a fun conversation. Atis Shala: Definitely. Considering you joined crypto in 2013, if I'm not mistaken, this is going to be a long one. Before we get into everything else, I want to ask you the question I ask everyone: what got you into crypto? What was the idea behind you joining? It's a whole world out there, and crypto has changed so much over the years. Corey Petty: I might take up our whole time with this one. I originally did a PhD in computational physics, and I've always been fascinated with computation. My PhD was in high-performance computing, so solving really hard computational problems was something I cared about. I've also always been a deconstructionist: I like taking things apart and putting them back together with as few pieces as possible. By happenstance, I saw a TED talk about Bitcoin while I was doing my graduate studies, and I was fascinated by it. I liked the computational problem it was solving, the Byzantine Generals' Problem, and I thought the solution was elegant. So I researched it, wanted to understand the ins and outs, wanted to see how it could break down. Then I started playing with it, and I learned about money and the weirdness that is money. I found it fascinating that we'd built real, sovereign internet money, something we'd never had before. It was a fundamentally new thing to me, and I got lost in it. I started mining because the best way to learn is by doing, and the more competent I became, the more fascinated I got. Eventually, I started a podcast and met a lot of people through great conversations – that's The Bitcoin Podcast… shameless plug. I really enjoyed it, and eventually I left academia, because the problems I was solving there, while interesting, were problems nobody cared about. Meanwhile, this huge industry was emerging that I saw as an exponential technology about to take off, one that gives power back to people. I care a lot about cryptography, information, and decentralised systems, so I got a job doing data science and blockchain education, then moved into security. Then I got a job at Status after their ICO, where I was lead security engineer and CSO. I kept doing it because the ecosystem kept exploding, and I was always trying to build things I believe in: resilient systems built for adversarial settings, resistant to being taken over. That's core to who I am: figuring out how to build systems that aren't asymmetric in power. Dren Hima: I resonate with that. When we joined crypto, we were drawn in by the same philosophy. You've lived through the most important cycles this space has seen and watched it evolve into what it is today. Do you like it? Did you predict this is where it would end up? It doesn't feel the same anymore. I get nostalgic about a lot of things, but especially about when we first joined crypto. We can talk all day about ideology and institutions, but it just doesn't feel the same. I want your take, because I know you've been critical of the institutionalisation of crypto. Corey Petty: No, I don't like it, but I'm not surprised by it either. The ideology isn't gone. When we started The Bitcoin Podcast, our whole line was "adoption is the only thing that matters." We were going to replace the banks, give people ownership of their own financial data. But that's not the adoption we got, because it's genuinely hard to do. Using a wallet, taking responsibility for your own private keys, understanding what you're signing, understanding what chain your tokens are on, navigating the weird dynamics of DeFi – all of that is hard, and people don't like hard. It means learning something new and changing their behaviour. So the adoption we got was driven by scale and convenience, and a lot of what we built ended up being the same thing we already had, just on the internet: traditional finance, online. That isn't what I signed up for, but it's clearly the direction things went, because it's what people wanted. We haven't yet convinced them of the thing I got into this for, and why they need it. I think we're getting there. People are starting to realise this isn't fundamentally different from what came before. I'm still hopeful we can build something that actually feels better than what we already have. Atis Shala: On the institutionalisation of crypto, I think it was inevitable, like you said. But I also think we asked for it, in a way. Maybe not you specifically, but the majority of the industry. Back in 2020 and 2021, whenever there was news of some new institution getting into crypto, everyone got fired up. I think the industry has an identity crisis around this, and it connects to privacy too, because I think anonymity and privacy in crypto should be non-negotiable. Corey Petty: I'd agree. Atis Shala: But how realistic is that? Regular people don't really care, do they? If you ask my parents whether they care that their data gets sold from their social media accounts to feed algorithms that essentially enslave them digitally, they wouldn't care. I try to say I care, and I try to stand behind the movement, but it's hard to stay idealistic in today's world. How would you convince someone to fight this fight? I see it almost as a war: How do you get people to stand behind these values? Corey Petty: That's a hard one. Honestly, I don't think you convince most people directly. This mirrors something I saw doing security work: people only care about security once it's already been breached, once it personally affects them, and by then it's usually too late. So, as builders, we have to be the ideological ones and build things that don't give people the option to skip these protections. It has to be built into the substrate, the infrastructure itself, so people are protected by default and have to actively opt out if they want to. That's consent, versus the current model, where consent was never really given. Privacy is the same story. The transparency baked into everything we use today creates a surveillance economy, and the easiest way to profit from that is to aggregate data and exploit it; the user becomes the product. Companies aren't building for what users need; they're building to take advantage of them, because that's what the current substrate incentivises. So I'm less interested in trying to "sell" privacy and anonymity, and more interested in building a substrate that doesn't give people that choice to be exploited by default, one where they have to actively consent, and in some cases can even profit from their own data instead of someone else scraping it because that's the cheapest option. You can't bolt privacy onto a system after the fact – or you can, but it's much harder. The lifecycle of a transaction has many steps, and if you think of the blockchain as the settlement layer, that's the end of the lifecycle. Almost all the surveillance and profiteering happens before you ever get there. So it doesn't matter if you have a privacy solution on the blockchain if everything's already been harvested upstream, or if bad actors just go after whoever's using the privacy solution instead. You have to secure and privatise the entire transaction lifecycle, so the user can choose when to disclose information, instead of having it sold off before they ever had a choice. Dren Hima: That's exactly it. People did ask for mass adoption. They did ask for institutional money to come in. It's like asking for rain and getting a thunderstorm instead. Corey Petty: A monsoon. Dren Hima: A monsoon with a lot of narratives and political battles thrown in, though we don't need to go down that rabbit hole right now. I want to ask about Logos and the philosophy behind it. You mentioned pivoting away from academia. I imagine you had to unlearn a fair amount from that world to get to where you are now, building Logos and everything that comes with it. Corey Petty: I don't know that I've unlearned so much as stopped using it the way I originally learned it. I've actually come full circle on this: I think institutions really matter. But you need to build good ones, because institutions are what survive across generations; they carry forward core ideas and complex thought, and train new people to keep doing that. So you need to rebuild institutions in a way that makes them uncapturable, which requires the right infrastructure underneath them. What we mostly see today are captured institutions. The goal is to rebuild them so they're resistant to capture. That's what we've been trying to do with blockchains: build technology that resists this asymmetric dynamic where a small number of people end up controlling the whole system. We've learned a lot over the past decade and a half about how to actually do that well, and maybe now we're at a point where we can build something that genuinely helps rebuild institutions in society. Atis Shala: So, how do you actually plan to do that? Institutions keep getting built in ways that are easy to capture. I don't want to be the pessimist here, but it feels like almost anything can be bought with today's mindset – a lot of people are losing their ideals. Everyone you talk to about building something better ends up asking, "What's in it for me, financially?" I get it, it's a business, but we're trying to build something with a different kind of value, not just financial. How do you want to change that? Corey Petty: A lot of our philosophy is: don't try to fix the existing system, build something in parallel that gives people options, purpose-built for what they actually need, instead of trying to bend something that was never designed to serve them. And you have to build those things so they can't easily be captured or broken. That means resilient technology that gives people the tools to build their own communities and parallel institutions in their own niche areas, and then supports that growth. Ideally, what emerges are resilient institutions that actually serve real people, instead of the detached systems we have now. It starts with building technology that's provably resistant in real-world conditions, then going out, learning people's actual problems, and helping them build things that serve those needs, then fostering that community growth. I don't think you get real societal change unless you do both simultaneously: build uncapturable technology that serves people, and understand people's problems well enough to help them use it. Big problems only get solved by big communities, so you have to battle-test this stuff, let it grow iteratively, and keep the focus on actually helping people. Dren Hima: As an economist myself, I put some blame on economists for this. We tend to assign statistical value to almost everything except privacy. You see projects shipping surveillance tracking in the backend that users have no idea about. But if you asked people how much they'd pay to have their data protected and be anonymous online, I'd bet most would pay something. So privacy can be monetised too. Which brings me to AI. It's scaled a lot of good things, but also a lot of the bad, including surveillance. I'll be honest, Claude and ChatGPT know a lot about me because I'm the type of person who asks for help with the most minor things. I vouch for total privacy, and yet I'm clearly caught up in this too. I want to hear your take on AI. You've written about how it boosts efficiency, but are there hidden dynamics people aren't aware of, beyond surveillance and privacy? Corey Petty: That's a big one. I'm fascinated by AI for a lot of reasons: how it works, the emergent property of it actually being able to reason, the environmental and social implications of hyperscalers, how people use and leverage it, and whether it makes them stop thinking or actually think better and become more efficient. What worries me is the amount of control these hyperscalers actually have, and the potential, from that control, to manipulate society in ways that aren't obvious. You ask it questions the way you'd use a search engine, and it gives you an answer, but you don't know where that answer really comes from. It comes from how the model was trained, post-trained, served, and the rules the provider builds in. This is the first time in history a single company controls the entire information pipeline – from data aggregation to training to serving – and it's all proprietary. You don't really know how any of it works. Historically, we've had multiple institutions and gatekeepers controlling different parts of an information pipeline, which gave us some checks and balances. That's gone now. These companies are also transnational and massive, so they're not really subject to any single jurisdiction. It's a scary, unproven situation. AI has real potential to make society better, but only if it's built with checks and balances we haven't figured out yet, and I don't think hyperscalers are the ones who'll figure it out. We also haven't solved how to make these systems capable enough without just scaling them bigger and bigger, with all the resources that requires. So there's real potential for harm and real potential for good, and I'm caught in the middle. Computationally, it's fascinating. I love it, it makes me better at what I do, it helps me learn. But it can also make people dumber if they don't use it the right way. We'll see. Atis Shala: I saw a post somewhere – "don't outsource your thinking to AI" – and honestly, I think I've been doing exactly that. Corey Petty: Because a lot of the value in life is in the thinking itself. Struggling with an idea, wrestling with complexity – that's the point of the exercise. When you offload that entirely, you lose the capacity to do it. Atis Shala: I think at some point you stop being human, in a sense. After a decade of outsourcing everything to AI, people just forget how to think, and that's the one thing that makes us human. I don't want to go too far down that road either. So, you said you're fascinated by AI, but how do we stay decentralised and keep these giants from taking over? Is local compute the answer to AI sovereignty, or are we too far from that? Corey Petty: I think we'll find ways to decentralise training, inference, and data ownership and aggregation – the whole pipeline that feeds these models. Model sizes will shrink to the point where meaningful reasoning can run on devices people can actually afford, so it stops being a global scarcity problem over who controls the compute. It becomes something you can run on your laptop or phone, once we get better at doing this efficiently. At that point, you're no longer dependent on hyperscalers, because there's an alternative. I've made this comparison with crypto before: I don't mind using Coinbase, because it's built on a decentralised platform. If I don't like what they're doing with my Bitcoin, I can move it onto the blockchain directly. I have the option to exit. If you don't have that option, a company can do whatever it wants, because you can't do anything about it. So whether we're talking about crypto or AI, you need a place to exit – a way to still do what you want to do, without being subject to any one company's rules. When people have that option, companies have to earn their users because those users can simply leave. Atis Shala: I agree with all of that, but from your perspective, what role does blockchain play in a future where people run local, private AI? There have been a few blockchain projects aiming at more efficient data preservation than Bitcoin's chain, while keeping its core benefits. I remember one called MINA, back in 2021, though I'm not sure it still exists. I know the concept is out there, but is it actually being practised? Can blockchain support that future while staying private? Corey Petty: Absolutely, that's exactly what Logos is trying to do. Blockchain plays a critical role in building decentralised, resilient applications by providing meaningful digital scarcity: I can give you something, and you know I no longer have it, because of global total ordering that everyone can agree on. In an age where AI can manufacture almost anything, trustless verifiability becomes essential. I know something is mine, and it's provable – backed by cryptography, not by someone's word. Systems that operate reliably in adversarial conditions give me confidence something actually happened and that I can prove it. Add zero-knowledge proofs, and I can prove something happened correctly without revealing the underlying details. That combination – total ordering, verifiability, permissions, decentralisation that resists takeover, and privacy – is powerful. It matters when you work with people you don't fully trust, or when you're building communities that can't be captured because they don't leak the information needed to capture them. Blockchains serve that role, but you don't put real data on-chain. The chain is just there to prove something happened, for as long as you need that proof. After that, you can checkpoint and archive it elsewhere, because the cryptographic linkage already guarantees immutability. That's what something like Logos Storage is for: keeping large amounts of data available long-term while staying private. Where blockchains have historically lacked privacy is in the consensus and mining process itself, which leaks information and has led to people being coerced or robbed. So we believe privacy needs to be built in at the lowest level of the stack – where nodes actually run. I don't want to know your IP address, your stake, or your influence over the mining process; I just want to know the process is fair and verifiable. That's what we're doing with zero-knowledge proofs and what we call the Blend network – it hides who proposed a given block and also obscures the network forensics around how that block propagates. Even if you can't see what's inside the chain, existing "private" chains are still vulnerable because you can watch who's actually processing transactions and go after them. If you want this to hold up in the real world, privacy has to exist at the lowest level. We believe we've done that with Logos, but it still needs to be battle-tested and scaled. Dren Hima: How do we keep bad actors away? A lot of the case for surveillance states rests on the idea that privacy enables crime, because authorities can't track bad actors – that's where a lot of the pushback on privacy comes from. Is it realistic to build a world with real privacy that's still safe from bad actors, without undermining the principles that made privacy possible in the first place? Corey Petty: No, there will always be bad actors. There are bad actors today. The real question is whether the good this technology enables outweighs the harm those bad actors cause. I've always believed ethical people should be the ones building this technology, because if they aren't, the good guys end up playing catch-up to the bad actors' methods instead. Wherever a community reaches a certain size, you'll find people trying to exploit it; that's just how it goes. You build systems that minimise their impact and structure networks so no one can assert outsized control, because bad actors aren't going away. You want ethical builders creating the tools, and you help the people trying to stop bad actors by understanding how bad actors could exploit the system. A lot of what bad actors need is information. If you don't hand it to them, it becomes much harder to do what they want to do, especially anything involving surveillance or exploitation of others. So no, you don't eliminate bad actors, but you build systems resilient to them, and help the communities using the technology root out bad behaviour where it exists. At the end of the day, it's humans on both sides of this technology, and humans make mistakes; you catch bad actors not by manipulating the system, but by watching the humans. Dren Hima: I want to talk about the concept of parallel societies. What's the most concrete evidence, in your view, that parallel societies are real and not just a metaphor? Corey Petty: That's really more Jarrad's territory; it's his whole thing. But I can offer a few examples. We already have special economic zones, which function as financially incentivised parallel societies outside normal jurisdictions. Unconventional communities are operating in international waters, doing their own thing – a modern echo of how piracy historically forced questions about jurisdiction and jurisdiction-free spaces. And throughout history, we've seen parallel institutions stand up to regimes and win – not through violence. It's hard for me to push my own views here because I've always focused on the technology side of this. I like the idea of people having a right to exit, and spending their time in systems that actually benefit them instead of exploiting them. Jarrad's book,  Farewell to Westphalia , has great examples of parallel institutions throughout history that worked: economically viable, sometimes producing real markets worth pursuing. This isn't just an idealistic social movement; there's real business opportunity in serving people this way. But I don't spend my time studying that side these days. I'm more focused on what emerges once we give people the technology to build it themselves. Atis Shala: Let's look at the future of Logos. You have three products: Messaging, Storage, and Blockchain. What's still missing from the stack right now? I think the unification of the brand happened in late 2025. What's the next step, and what should people following Logos be excited about? Corey Petty: We have testnets running, and most of the four core pieces are working: execution environments with DEXs, private atomic swaps, all the main components. Now we need to harden them, test them, and grow the user base building on top of them. The best thing anyone can do is download Basecamp, run a node, and either file a bug report or try to break it – or build something on top of it. We have grant programmes and RFPs for people who want to help build, so it's not just us building this and handing it to people – it's meant to be a community effort. The best measure of success, honestly, is someone building something we never planned for. You can start today: download Basecamp, check the website, and look at the funded opportunities for things we want built but don't have the time or resources for ourselves. Running a node is genuinely simple: download Basecamp, click run, and it can run on something as small as a Raspberry Pi. We have things in the pipeline to make that even easier, so you're not limited to running it on your main machine – you can deploy it to a small device at home, or rely on someone else's node safely, because our light-client protocols let you verify the data you're being given is correct. Atis Shala: So, through the Lambda programme, I could go build something like Logos Markets – a prediction market – and get funded? Corey Petty: If your proposal is solid, yes, we'll fund you. Atis Shala: I might need your help putting that proposal together. Corey Petty: Submit a proposal; the requirements are laid out clearly. I actually helped build the evaluation framework, so when people build something, they know exactly what they're building against, and it's easy to check whether it meets the bar. We want people doing this; we've allocated funding for it, because you can't do this alone. You need people building on it, with a real stake in growing the network alongside you. Dren Hima: Zooming out – ten years from now, ignoring PR metrics and TVL numbers that have flooded my feed – what would tell you Logos succeeded? And what would tell you it didn't? Corey Petty: Success, to me, looks like large communities actually using the Logos stack to run something they need – a land registry, a local market, a voting system, something meaningful and community-scale. That's real impact. I don't want to see another DeFi protocol that just shuffles money around and profits someone without doing anything else. I want real societal impact, and people getting curious enough to build new kinds of communities on top of it – genuine parallel societies, meaning communities of like-minded people who've opted in around shared values. As those grow, they need some form of bureaucracy to hold together, and the technology can serve that through registries, fair markets, voting mechanisms, and so on. That's success. Failure looks like exactly where we are today – regulated stablecoins that don't actually serve people. Atis Shala: I want to ask about Blend, since it's relatively new to Logos, and you mentioned how easy node setup is supposed to be. What's your plan for growing adoption of Blend nodes? It's a brutal market to grow in right now. Corey Petty: Great question. This is something I've always cared about, because privacy exists in proportion to the size of the anonymity set, and there's a real bootstrapping problem: How do you build and maintain that set? Here's the short version of how Blend works today: when someone wins the right to propose the next block in Cryptarchia, our consensus mechanism, they have to broadcast it to the network – and that broadcast leaks information. Over time, someone doing network forensics could de-anonymise who holds what stake just by observing how often they propose blocks, since proposal frequency is weighted by stake. That could expose someone's IP address and, ultimately, their physical location, which we obviously want to avoid. Blend solves this by routing proposals through a network inspired by mix nets – though it isn't quite a mix net – introducing random delays across multiple hops, where each hop doesn't know who came before it. That hides who's submitting what. But you also need cover traffic, so not every message looks like a block proposal, or you can trivially tell which messages actually matter. Plain cover traffic, though, is just wasted bandwidth. There's something new on the roadmap I'm comfortable discussing now, called EmPoWering – a neat way to solve several of these problems at once. The economics aren't fully worked out yet, but I'm writing that up now. The rough idea: a new node could do proof-of-work to hit a certain threshold and generate a small pool of funds that covers their first transaction on the Blend network, meaning you can gain entry and keep the anonymity set alive purely by contributing computation, without needing outside funding. This incentivises fresh accounts to submit real transactions instead of relying on synthetic cover traffic, and you can auto-tune the size of the anonymity set the same way Bitcoin auto-tunes mining difficulty, matching it against real network traffic. That gives us real cover traffic made of genuine transactions, funded by proof-of-work rather than some external funding source that would otherwise dox you – say, by requiring a deposit from an exchange. It solves the bootstrapping problem: How do you enter proof-of-stake consensus without funding your node from a traceable source? You should be able to enter and exit the network freely, the same way you can with Bitcoin mining, without needing to fund anything up front. It's a genuinely new approach. Version three of Blend should include an early implementation in testnet, though the documentation isn't public yet. I'm writing a technical piece that covers the economics in more depth. Atis Shala: So it's essentially a modular way to enter the Blend network. Corey Petty: Right – it automatically tunes the security and efficiency of the anonymity set, and gives people an onboarding path that doesn't require funding a node before they can send a single transaction. You can mine your way into your first transaction. Atis Shala: Looking forward to that write-up. Dren Hima: How do we get the average degen trader into Logos? Privacy as a narrative is arguably having its best year yet: ZEC has had a moment, Monero keeps coming up, and there are more privacy-by-default chains launching. But how do we make it stick and bring in the next wave of users? We've had Session on the podcast before – a decentralised alternative to Telegram – and they're relying on donations because it's hard to scale something with real utility without eventually needing the average degen trader in the network. Corey Petty: We need trading activity; things need to move for any of this to be sustainable, and people need to use it. Dren Hima: Exactly, so how do we bring them in? Corey Petty: I don't have a full solution, but I have ideas. One is building something efficient enough to support applications that genuinely can't be built elsewhere: a fully private transaction lifecycle that doesn't require negotiating a multisig transaction over Telegram, real private atomic swaps, and so on. Another is a developer experience that's second to none and unified across the whole ecosystem – interacting with Storage feels similar to interacting with Messaging, which feels similar to interacting with the blockchain layer. Because these pieces are merged, we can offer a seamless experience for building an entire application – chat, long-term storage, consensus, token swaps – all within one wallet, one integrated system. If the infrastructure is solid and the developer experience is genuinely simple – without the usual glue code of stitching together Ethereum for one thing and Solana for swaps and something else for storage – that complexity mostly disappears. Good infrastructure, real guarantees, real control over when to disclose information, and ease of building on top of it: that's how you get people to build the applications that eventually pull in that next wave of users. Atis Shala: Suppose you succeed in driving privacy adoption and build out a whole ecosystem around it, similar to what already exists for non-private blockchains, and then a government decides to ban anything connected to privacy platforms, threatening serious jail time for users, and other countries follow suit. Realistically, what can we do? I know Monero was recently delisted from most major exchanges. Is enough being done to engage policymakers and convince them that some of these regulatory approaches to privacy are wrong? Corey Petty: I don't know how to solve politics. It matters a great deal because those decisions affect so many people. Even if the technology works perfectly, if using it becomes practically unusable because of the legal consequences, you won't get adoption: people will be too scared to use it. That's not a problem you fix by building better technology; it's a problem you fix by talking to people – your local representatives, your community. Ideally, when one jurisdiction gets something wrong, others call it out. Public pressure and reputational cost are really the only tools that have consistently worked to change behaviour, but that requires global coordination and people actually caring. Part of our job, as builders, is proving this technology is genuinely good for people, so they demand it and go tell their own local representatives why they care. Without that grassroots demand, you don't get real political change – and to get that grassroots demand, we have to show people solutions that meaningfully improve their lives, not just talk about ideals. Dren Hima: We've had a lot of guests on this show who are polished and media-trained, saying what they know how to say. It's rare to get someone who genuinely knows what they're talking about. Dr Corey Petty, thank you so much for joining us. This has been a genuinely eye-opening conversation, and I wish we had more time, because there's so much more we could dig into. Corey Petty: Thank you, I appreciate that. There's so much to talk about; it's a fascinating space. Dren Hima: It really is the most interesting industry in the world – chaotic; sometimes I question why I joined, but here we are, building asshole-resistant technology. Cheers to that. Corey Petty: Thank you for having me; this was great! Dren Hima: Thank you.

documents.title: Logos Dev Update: July 2026
documents.description: Your monthly update on the development of the Logos technology stack.
documents.body: Logos provides monthly updates on the state of the technology stack and the development of its various modules, giving developers a clear snapshot of what has been built over the past month. For developer-focused highlights on X, please follow  Logos Tech . For broader updates on the Logos movement as a whole, stay tuned to the main  Logos account. Anonymous messaging over the mix network The month's most significant milestone was making sender-anonymous messaging a capability developers can pick up and use. LIONESS payload encryption for Sphinx was merged into the mix protocol implementation and confirmed to integrate with Logos Delivery without issues, preserving message integrity end to end. Documentation was then published covering  how to send anonymised messages over the mix network on testnet v0.2, with messages routed sender-unlinkably through a three-hop mixnet via Logos Chat. Mix-based chat with DoS protection was also presented and demoed at the  IFT Town Hall . Logos technology stack updates Logos Core Basecamp moved to a dockable workspace layout, added keyboard shortcut handling and an ARM Linux build, and now presents a single install and upgrade confirmation dialog listing any dependency changes. Storage Storage research focused on hidden services, with a purpose-built simulator developed to model a hidden service over the mix network using guards and vanguards, followed by a free-route simulator for studying path selection and the malicious-path problem. Work also progressed on NAT traversal ahead of Testnet v0.2.1, with several improvements made that significantly improve node connectivity. Elsewhere, all wire protocols were migrated to nim-protobuf-serialisation in place of hand-written serialisers, and the Logos Storage UI was brought largely into line with the Logos Design System. Messaging The Messaging API progressed closer towards main feature completeness. RLN was isolated into a self-contained module usable by any protocol, the FFI node lifecycle was unified and the legacy surface dropped, structured API layers were introduced, and an in-repo end-to-end test suite was added. Logos Chat advanced towards Beta with GroupV2 client integration, group names and descriptions, membership changes surfaced as events, and key bundles now published over Logos Delivery. The Reliable Channel API continued to stabilise, and the Rate Limit Manager moved into the messaging client layer. Blockchain Testnet v0.2 completed its rollout across the stack, with the Logos Blockchain node 0.2.0 released alongside the blockchain module and dashboard, the LEZ module, wallet UI, indexer, and explorer. An iterative update, Testnet v0.2.1, is expected to roll out on 5 August 2026. On the Logos Execution Zone, a Keccak speedup for the Risc0 backend cut proving time by roughly half, and async cross-zone messaging reached review complete with a browser demo showing send, finalise, and receive timings live. Nimbos merged libp2p AutoNAT v2 and wired SDP validator operations into the ledger. AnonComms Two long-running research threads reached publication. The  oracle mechanism specification is now published as a LIP, laying the groundwork for the Decentralised Oracle Network, and the  payment streams on-chain specification was published alongside an end-to-end demo of payment streams with Store integration. The Zerokit v3.0.0 rearchitecture is close to release, and a working RLN membership management module and UI were deployed on testnet, including an experiment using a Keycard device certificate as an authentication method. Post-quantum benchmarks and research Post-quantum work continued to be a recurring theme, with benchmarks of cryptographic primitives conducted on a Raspberry Pi 5 and Apple M3, and Blend post-quantum primitive candidates finalised. An anonymous communications simulation framework with two closed-form anonymity predictions was built, a survey of turn-assignment mechanisms for channel sequencing was completed, and the Checkpoint-based Fast Bootstrapping RFC was opened for review. Documentation Logos Storage documentation is being revamped, with a view to eventually add it to the documentations available on  docs.logos.co . A set of runnable tutorials was also added to the libp2p module, with continuous integration checks on the tutorial code. A closer look at the user-facing launcher for the Logos stack was also published in  Basecamp in Testnet v0.2 . The documentation for the Logos stack is maintained at  docs.logos.co , and the  Node Operator Guide remains the best starting point for running a node on Logos Testnet v0.2. Logos Broadcast Network and Circles Throughout July, Logos contributors continued to host online and IRL Circles around the world, creating digital and physical space to solve real-world problems with privacy-preserving technology. Logos contributors  also headed to DWeb in Berlin last month , where we hosted four days of talks, technical sessions, and fostering collective action to support human freedom. Check out  this recap of the event on X . The Logos Broadcast Network continued to deliver regular programming, from Dev Club sessions and weekly technical updates to office hours every Friday at 14:00 UTC. Join these office hours to learn more about building on the Logos stack or to get help with specific issues. To help new users get started with downloading and using Basecamp, Logos has  published a set of tutorials on YouTube . Full schedules and participation details are available at  press.logos.co/calendar and  logos.co/circles . For a full list of upcoming Logos events, check out the event page on  Luma . To get the latest developer updates from the Logos stack, follow  Logos Tech on X. Stay tuned to the main  Logos account for news on the wider global movement.

documents.title: Interzone Bridging: Moving Value Between Zones on Logos
documents.description: How Logos Zones move tokens and messages between each other without a trusted intermediary.
documents.body: Bridges have been the most expensive thing in this industry to get wrong. Ronin lost roughly $620 million in March 2022 when five of its nine validator keys were compromised. Wormhole had lost $325 million seven weeks earlier to a signature verification flaw. Harmony's Horizon bridge lost close to $100 million on a two-of-five multisig that summer, Nomad around $190 million a month after that, and Multichain about $126 million in 2023 after its team lost access to the keys holding the pools. Cumulative losses across cross-chain bridges run into the billions. The causes differ in the detail, but the underlying challenge is the same. Something has to stand between two chains and attest that a deposit happened on the far side, and that something — a relayer, a multisig committee, an MPC keyset — becomes the most valuable target in the system. Compromise the attestor and you are able to mint whatever you like. Whether it is a cross-chain bridge or a cross-Zone transfer, this mechanism extends the supply chain of a transaction and consequently its privacy exposure surface. Conventional cross-chain bridges mitigate this exposure by inserting a party that both chains agree to believe, but protection is only ever as strong as its weakest link. In nearly every bridge that has been drained, that trusted party was exploited. So now that Logos Zones can move tokens and messages between one another, the obvious question is: how does that work without a trusted intermediary? What shipped PR #542 landed on 11 July: asynchronous cross-Zone messaging between Logos Execution Zone (LEZ) instances, with two demos running on one shared messaging spine. The first is a minimal ping between Zones. The second locks tokens on Zone A and mints a wrapped representation on Zone B. There is also a two-Zone chat app that sends messages across and displays send, finalise and receive timings live in the browser. This work is called “interzone bridging", but the mechanics have little in common with what bridging between different blockchains normally means. Here, it refers not to moving tokens between different networks, but different Zones that are designed to be interoperable and linked to the Logos base layer. The shared base layer Zones are customisable execution environments that lean on the Logos blockchain for consensus and data availability. The  documentation covers what a Zone is and how  Mantle channels anchor Zone state to the chain . A key property of this architecture is that every Zone reads the same finalised blocks. Traditional bridges connect chains that share nothing. Ethereum has no idea what Solana’s state is, so somebody has to carry the news across, and that somebody has to be trusted. Every bridge design is some flavor of “who carries the news and why do we believe them.” Multisigs, oracle networks, light clients, they’re all answers to that question, and the first two have been the most expensive answers in the history of this industry. Logos Zones never face that question. Zone B does not need to be told what happened on Zone A, because Zone A's activity is already sitting in a finalised block that Zone B reads as a matter of course. How a message moves The token bridge demo below shows the flow most clearly. A program on Zone A locks the tokens and records an outbound message through a built-in outbox program. That message lands in a finalised block like any other Zone A activity. Zone B's sequencer runs a watcher over Zone A's finalised blocks. When the outbound message appears, the sequencer injects the delivery into Zone B as a sequencer-origin transaction, and the wrapped-token program mints. Zone B's indexer then re-derives that same delivery from the same finalised block, independently. Both Zones run identical LEZ code, so the indexer can reconstruct what the delivery must be, byte for byte, and throw out anything that does not match. Forged deliveries fail. Replayed deliveries fail. The verifier pins Zone A's block-signing keys, so a fabricated source chain fails too. This means the sequencer injecting the delivery is never trusted. It carries the delivery but holds no authority over it, because every injection is checked against what the finalised block says it must have been. A sequencer that injects invalid data gets its own block rejected by its own indexer. There is no relayer committee here, no multisig, no oracle, no extra validator set, no new token to stake. Verification is re-derivation from finalised state, so the trust model of interzone bridging is simply the trust model of the chain underneath it. Nothing crosses between the two Zones, because both of them are already reading the same blocks. Sequencing and atomic coordination Two related threads of work make this picture more complete. Sequencer decentralisation is the first. Today’s design gives sequencers a job (watch, inject) but no authority (the indexer verifies everything). The team is reworking zone sequencing toward stake-gated registration with round-robin turns and posting timeouts, so no single sequencer can stall a zone, and by extension stall its cross-zone deliveries. A malicious sequencer can’t forge deliveries now; a decentralised set means one can’t withhold them either. Second, async messaging is one half of cross-zone interaction. The other half is the Cross-Zone Atomic Coordination Protocol, a four-phase off-chain protocol (intent proposal, verification, signature exchange, submission) for the synchronous case where two zones need to commit a transaction atomically. Both sequencers hold a complete signed transaction after the signature exchange, which removes the single point of failure of classical two-phase commit. That work is still at the specification stage, with a security analysis covering abort scenarios at each phase. Either way, the principle is the same one the rest of the Logos stack is built on. Every link in the chain gets verified on its own terms rather than inherited on trust from the link before it, which is why one compromised component draining everything is not a failure mode this architecture has. Scope and limitations This is LEZ-to-LEZ only. Both Zones running identical code is the premise that makes byte-for-byte re-derivation possible at all. Bridging to arbitrary external chains is a different problem and this work makes no claim on it. Cross-Zone messaging is opt-in and off by default. A Zone with no cross-Zone configuration behaves exactly as it did before. This is also the first part of a larger design. Follow-up work will include generalised message envelopes, an emitter-agnostic watcher, refund handling, and a broader trust and discovery model beyond the two demo flows. This mechanism is purely Zone-to-Zone: moving tokens between the Logos blockchain and a single Zone is a separate system, already live, built on Mantle channel deposits and withdrawals and  covered in the documentation . Get involved To try interzone bridging: Run the two-Zone demo from the  PR , send messages between Zones, and watch the timings in the chat app; Read the indexer-side verifier and the integration tests covering forgery, replay and ingress guarding, then open an issue if there is a hole in the design; Or  work through the documentation for more on Zones, channels, and how Zone state is anchored to the chain. Build the parallel. Prove it in practice. Keep it human.

documents.title: State of the Logos Network: July 2026
documents.description: Your roundup of recent developments from the Logos social movement and tech stack
documents.body: Testnet v0.2 now live Logos Testnet v0.2 launched on 30 June and, after several weeks of testing and hardening, we began its wider promotion last month. The release strengthens the core Logos Messaging, Storage, and Blockchain modules while bringing foundational privacy features online. Key updates include the Blend Network for  block proposer anonymity , token bridging between sovereign Zones, decentralised sequencing, improved message delivery, and NAT traversal. All core modules are now available through Logos Basecamp, making it easier to run a node, join the testnet, and start building privacy-preserving applications. Learn more and run  Logos Basecamp . Bota Jardemalie on the need for private infrastructure In 2013, Kazakh lawyer Bota Jardemalie took a Skype call from a client whose testimony exposed how vulnerable communication channels can be. Soon after, she says she was publicly branded a criminal, placed on an Interpol red notice, targeted by surveillance and kidnapping attempts, and pressured through a years-long legal campaign and the detention of her brother. Logos Broadcast Network spoke to Bota, who shared her story and reiterated the importance of secure communication channels:  “If you don’t control your channel of communication, you become extremely vulnerable.”  She also outlined the kind of tools and infrastructure our freedoms hinge on: private communication, censorship-resistant records, and payments that cannot be frozen or traced. We’re building Logos to protect people like Bota, as well as anyone else who might need private-by-default infrastructure. Medusa wallet live on Logos Medusa is a private, self-custodial wallet built for Logos Blockchain by developer ParadoxComputer. Available as a Logos Basecamp module, it supports multiple identities within one wallet and is designed to hold and move value across Logos zones. ParadoxComputer describes it as a “MetaMask for Logos.” In their own words: “One wallet, many identities. Hold and move value across every Logos zone with shielded, self-custodial privacy, and let dapps connect only with your say-so.” Medusa supports features including shielded transactions, private addresses and multiple-address management. It is part of ParadoxComputer’s wider development work on Logos, which also includes  LEZ ZoneScan , an explorer for the Logos Execution Zone. See the code or  check out Medusa on Logos now . Medusa wallet was developed independently using Logos tech. Do your own due diligence before installing. Jarrad Hope on Unchained Laura Shin’s  Unchained podcast brought together Jarrad Hope of Logos, Joe Andrews of Aztec Labs, and Mert Mumtaz of Helius to discuss why privacy is becoming one of crypto’s most important frontiers. The conversation covered the challenges of building privacy technology, including Zcash’s long-undetected counterfeit vulnerability, the quantum threat to crypto, regulatory pressure, and the difference between cryptographic privacy and systems that still rely on trusted intermediaries. Jarrad focused on privacy as a requirement for the entire transaction lifecycle. He argued that communication, network access, and other layers can expose users and institutions even when the blockchain itself offers strong settlement guarantees. He also introduced the audience to the Logos tech stack as a solution to leaks at links in the transaction supply chain beyond settlement. IRL / Upcoming Logos LAN and Circles / Zanzalu Logos returned to Zanzalu in Zanzibar from 25 July to 14 August, building on the  Circle formed there last year . Logos Circle / Zanzalu identified a lack of access to computer education as a winnable issue and raised funds to equip the Straight Training Center with Raspberry Pis and other learning tools.  This year’s activities look set to include a volunteer day at the centre, hands-on training for new Circle stewards, and workshops introducing participants to Logos Basecamp and to running a Logos node.  Africa Privacy Conference We’ll also be at the  Africa Privacy Conference , now scheduled for mid-September. At the Logos booth, attendees can explore Basecamp, receive support with running a node, and learn how to participate in Logos Circle / Benin’s ongoing actions. The event is also an opportunity to connect with prospective Circle stewards and strengthen the African Logos community. IRL / July DWeb Camp DWeb Camp took place in the Alte Hölle forest in early July, shortly after the Logos Testnet v0.2 launch. An aligned audience, still largely unfamiliar with Logos’s work, was invited to explore the underlying vision and tech stack through a series of sessions.  Across the camp, Logos hosted a Basecamp presentation; Demo Night demonstrations of technology already being built on Logos, including the Meshtastic and radio modules; a live Keycard demonstration; and a presentation on decentralised libraries. A hands-on Pop-Up Circle session invited participants to identify a concrete, winnable issue and coordinate action around it, giving a practical feel of what activism within Logos Circles can look like. Logos also stayed on to help pack down the camp and leave the forest as it was found.  Look out for more practical tech demonstrations and movement activations at aligned events in the future. Logos Circles / July Highlights Logos Circles bring people together in locally organised, open groups focused on practical action. Participants identify challenges in their communities and develop grassroots projects to address them, forming a growing global network of local initiatives that adopt Logos tech where useful.  More about Circles Find a Circle near you Propose a new  Circle In July, Circles formed in: / Lisbon / Awka / Kano / Ede / Abeokuta / Delhi / Ebonyi / Abuja / Zanzibar / Kampala / Delta / Mumbai / Vizag / Benin / Los Angeles / Zanzibar / Ruse / Gombe / Wukari / Lagos / Madrid / Calabar / Aba / London / Uyo / Yola / Port Harcourt / Ibadan / Kaduna / Katsina Check the Logos Forum for individual progress updates on each Circle’s winnable issues. New steward onboarding programme We just launched a new training programme designed for those who want to start a Logos Circle in their area. It’s a self-paced course that should only take a couple of hours to complete and aims to prepare would-be Circle stewards to embark on their journey. If you’re interested in being involved,  please reach out to us . Logos Circle / Delhi supporting parallel education In July, Logos Circle / Delhi supported a volunteer-run, open-air learning programme for children underserved by formal schooling. Members visited a class, spoke with volunteers and students, and distributed notebooks and learning materials. The Circle is now helping turn the initiative into a more stable community learning hub by organising regular tutors, tracking attendance and progress, securing recurring supplies, and finding a weatherproof teaching space.  Learn more . Cleaning up Vizag Logos Circle / Vizag completed its first winnable issue by leading a community cleanup of RK Beach in July. Members collected plastic and other waste, coordinated its removal with local authorities, and spoke with beach visitors about coastal pollution. Several passers-by also joined the effort. Afterwards, the group shared breakfast and discussed future priorities for Vizag, including student mentoring and local issue reporting.  Learn more. Logos Circles / August Logos Circles are already planned in the cities below in August: / Awka (1 Aug):  Get involved. / Lisbon (1 Aug):  Get involved .  / Kano (8 Aug):  Get involved . / Abeokuta (14 Aug):  Get involved . Many Logos Circles are still finalising plans for their August gatherings, so only a few dates have been confirmed so far. Check the  Logos events calendar or the  Circles discussion channel later in the month for updates on upcoming Circles in your area.  If there isn’t already a Circle near you,  get involved and start one . Tech stack highlights In July, anonymous messaging over the mix network became usable and documented for the first time, with sender-anonymous messages now routed through a three-hop mixnet via Logos Chat.  LIONESS payload encryption was merged into the mix protocol and confirmed to work with Logos Delivery, and a demo of mix-based chat with DoS protection was implemented.  This followed June's Testnet v0.2 release, with the month spent consolidating progress across the wider stack, including Logos Core, storage, messaging, blockchain, and the Logos Execution Zone. Two long-running research threads also reached publication, with the oracle mechanism specification and the payment streams on-chain specification both released. Stay tuned for the July Logos developer update, which will be live on the Logos Blog very soon. Logos Blog Logos Blog publishes regular technical and activism updates, as well as philosophical writings about parallel organising and related fields. If there’s something you want to write about,  please reach out with a proposal .  In July, we published:  The Convergence Phase: A Testnet v0.1 Retrospective Building the Parallel Beside Logos Testnet v0.1 Logos Testnet v0.2: From Convergence to Architectural Readiness Logos Blockchain in Testnet v0.2: Privacy Reaches Consensus Bota Jardemalie on Surveillance, Exile, and Persecution Logos Broadcast Network Every month, the Logos Broadcast Network brings together live voices and ideas from across the movement. Its programming ranges from Logos Circle / Online and technical sessions for developers to conversations on alternative forms of organising and in-depth explorations of the Logos stack and related technologies.  Check the Logos Broadcast Network calendar to see upcoming streams . Ideas Thursdays are dedicated to the ideas on which Logos was founded. We welcome pioneering thinkers to discuss what they're working on and how it supports parallel organising. The latest addition to the LBN’s schedule is what we’re calling the Sovereignty Superspace. On the last Thursday of every month, we invite representatives from the various organisations Logos works with to discuss the most pressing issues in privacy, decentralised technology, and parallel organising. We hosted the first Sovereignty Superspace at the end of July.  Other July streams included:  The Future of Privacy (with Girl Gone Crypto) The War of Financial Privacy (with Aaron Day of Daylight Freedom Foundation) Good Enough Privacy? (with Paul Puey of Edge wallet) Apps Without a Kill Switch Sovereignty Superspace (with Nym’s Harry Halpin, DarkFi’s Amir Taaki, and Cake Wallet’s Seth) Follow  Logos on X or  YouTube to join these discussions every Thursday. Technical The Logos Broadcast Network also helps bring the developer community into the conversation through a dedicated schedule of technical streams. In July, the lineup featured:  Testnet v0.1 Retrospective Testnet v0.2 | Unstoppable Radio | Logos Dev Club We also released several shorts to help people get Logos technologies up and running. They included: Quickstart Logos Basecamp Installing Logos Basecamp Understanding .lgx Modules on Logos Basecamp Building Your First “Hello-World” UI Module on Logos Basecamp Follow  Logos Tech on X and subscribe to the  Logos YouTube channel to take part in all of our technical explorations and demos. Office hours Logos Office Hours are to help the community understand how to run and build on Logos. They take place weekly on Fridays at 12:00 UTC.  Put your questions directly to Logos engineers and deepen your understanding of the stack every week. Circles Logos Circle / Online brings together people who are solving local challenges in their communities each week. The sessions offer a practical look at how to create a Logos Circle, alongside firsthand lessons from participants already turning ideas into action.  Logos Circle / Online is on Tuesdays in English and every other Wednesday in Spanish. Join us   via the  Logos X account or  Logos YouTube channel. Community champions Logos is shaped by all its contributors. We celebrate the developers, engineers, thinkers, and changemakers whose code, ideas, and contributions push the mission forward and strengthen the movement.  Here are July’s community champions:  Shayan for their work on LogosUp and updating the Logos Circle / Lisbon node to Testnet v0.2. ParadoxComputer for their work on  Medusa wallet and other tools for Logos.  Devisha for their ongoing efforts and for supporting the formation of Logos Circle / Mumbai. Og_paka for building  TurboDex , a decentralised marketplace for AI agents running over Logos Messaging. Sai Kumar for organising the beach cleanup with Logos Circle / Vizag. All the stewards hosting Logos Circles in June, and everyone who attended. Anyone building on Logos tech. Everyone who listened to a Logos Broadcast Network stream or read a blog article. Everyone who joined us in DWeb Camp for Logos LAN and Pop-Up Circle. Your contribution could be included in a future community shoutout. Whether technical or non-technical, share meaningful work on  the forum or  Discord . Contribute where you can, build useful tools, and take the initiative.    We're building technologies and a social movement to revitalise civil society. We need developers, designers, writers, and activists to help shape it. Come build the parallel with us. Build on Logos.  Write for us. Join a Logos Circle.

documents.title: Bota Jardemalie on Surveillance, Exile, and Persecution
documents.description: What a decade of state persecution teaches about tools of surveillance and control.
documents.body: Companion piece to our interview with Bota Jardemalie.  Watch the full conversation here. Last week we sat down with Bota Jardemalie, a Kazakh human rights lawyer living under political asylum in Belgium. Near the end of the conversation she mentioned, almost in passing, that the European Parliament would vote the next day on reviving chat control, the legislation that lets platforms scan private messages. It had already been rejected twice, but this time she said they were using procedural tricks, and it would most likely pass. It passed. On July 9, 314 MEPs voted against reviving the scanning regime and 276 voted for it. It passed anyway, because rejection required an absolute majority of 361, and every absent member counted as a yes. Bota has spent over a decade learning exactly how systems like this get used once they exist. Her story is worth your time in full, but here is the outline of it. One intercepted Skype call Jardemalie is a Harvard Law graduate and a New York-qualified attorney. For years, she did international advocacy for the Kazakh opposition and victims of torture: bringing cases to the US State Department, Congress, the UN, anywhere a light could be shined on a regime that has no independent judiciary or press to shine one itself. In 2013, she took on the case of Alma Shalabayeva, the wife of a Kazakh opposition leader, who was grabbed along with her six-year-old daughter in a night raid in Italy, put on a private plane chartered by the Kazakh embassy, and flown to Kazakhstan. A UN expert called it an  extraordinary rendition . Kazakh diplomats had conspired with high-ranking Italian police officials to make it happen. The moment Shalabayeva landed in Kazakhstan, Jardemalie contacted her over Skype to take her testimony. First-hand testimony, recorded early, is what a case like this lives or dies on. They spent hours going through the details of the kidnapping. But the call was compromised. “I had such a big trust in technology,” she said. “I thought that if we’re on Skype, that’s it. It’s not like a landline. We can speak freely and nobody will know.” Within a week, her passport photo was on the front pages of Kazakh newspapers, framing her as a member of an organised criminal group. Within a month, she was on Interpol’s red notice list, an international fugitive, for doing what a lawyer is supposed to do: taking the testimony of a victim. She applied for asylum in Belgium because that’s where she was when she learned she was in danger, and that’s how asylum law works. “That taught me a very important lesson. You have to control your channel of communication. If you don’t control your channel of communication, you become extremely vulnerable to any abusers. It’s not necessarily the state. It can be a competitor.” One intercepted call was all it took. Punishment through procedure The case itself ended about as well as these things can. Shalabayeva and her daughter were released within six months and returned to Italy, where they received asylum. Six people were convicted of aggravated kidnapping. The scandal nearly collapsed the Italian government. What happened to Jardemalie afterward is a catalogue of what a state with unlimited resources can do to one person on Western soil, legally and otherwise: Belgium refused Kazakhstan’s extradition request. Interpol reviewed her file, recognised the persecution as politically motivated, and removed her from the database. So Kazakhstan hired people to kidnap her from Belgian territory instead. Belgian federal police caught them: two Germans and a Russian. The Germans were former Stasi officers, in their sixties, doing in retirement what they did before the Wall fell. A former UK Royal Marine rented the apartment across the street from hers, seventh floor facing seventh floor, and filmed inside her home. Her lawyers were hacked. A junior lawyer was approached with a bribe for her file. So was her real estate agent. When kidnapping didn’t work, her former employer, a Kazakh bank acting as a state proxy, filed a criminal complaint in Belgium accusing her of laundering half a billion dollars. The number was chosen to be outrageous enough that maybe a case would be opened and she would have to sit in pretrial detention for two years. The instructing judge dismissed it. They appealed and were dismissed. They appealed again – were dismissed again. Two law firms, one in Paris directing one in Brussels and ten years of procedure.  “Case dismissed, case dismissed, case dismissed, but they’re appealing, appealing, appealing. That’s what they’ve been doing to me. And it was legal.” At the appeal stage, Kazakhstan dumped thousands of pages of documents on the court, including what they claimed were her emails, recovered late, they said, from a hidden server. She opened the file properties, and the creation dates and author names were right there. “It was mind-blowing how reckless and how confident they were. Like nobody checks properties of files. I don’t know why people wouldn’t check. I checked.” And when none of that worked, they arrested her older brother in Kazakhstan, charged him with money laundering too, and told him he’d be released if he convinced his sister to come home. He refused. Two secret service officers took him from his cell to a basement. They made threats against his father, against his 20-year-old son. He suffered broken ribs, a mock hanging. He still refused. She asked him why, after his release (won through international pressure, including a bipartisan letter from the US Senate). He said: “I knew that if I cooperate, you probably come, and we both will never leave.” General-purpose tools of oppression It would be comfortable to file this under “authoritarian regimes are bad” and move on. Bota won’t let you. The mechanisms that were turned on her are general-purpose, and they’re not staying in Central Asia. Opposition movements in Kazakhstan can’t take funding from business people anymore, because business people who fund dissent lose their businesses. So movements run on crowdfunding, donations as small as $35. They used to post account information on social media, but they can’t now.  “The regime uses banks as their agent. Banks immediately freeze accounts used for any political purposes, the information is transferred to the secret service, and the secret service knows everyone who donated.” Activists moved to Bitcoin, Monero, whatever people were willing to use. After September 11, the regime’s charge of choice for activists was terrorism. Now, it’s money laundering.  “You don’t need to prove the underlying crime. As long as you have transactions, they can build something.” Everyone has a bank account, and a Western-trained lawyer accused of a financial crime is easy to sell. The definitions slide to fit the target: extremism covers a call to protest, money laundering covers a crowdfunding campaign, and what’s acceptable today gets reclassified tomorrow. Platforms operating in Kazakhstan are required by law to have in-country representatives, who remove “extremist” content on government request. Bota sees the same architecture going up in Europe under friendlier names. Harmful content under the Digital Services Act. Child protection under chat control.  “You create the tools. Those tools at some point will be used for broader purposes. As long as you’re creating this infrastructure, the government will have more and more appetite to use them.” Escape used to be geographic: people like Bota, like the families of many of us, escaped oppressive regimes by physically moving to freer countries. That exit is closing, not because the West is becoming Kazakhstan, but because it’s building infrastructure that centralises power and is capable of the same oppression. “They’re building the infrastructure. We don’t know what kind of people are going to come into power tomorrow. In some countries of the EU, we’re one election away from some quite authoritarian people coming into power.” The EU vote on chat control the next day passed, with 314 against, 276 for. Logos charts a new course Bota ended the interview with a request: “We need to work with developers who can explain why this type of attack on our privacy is dangerous.” So here’s our side of that handshake. At every point of her persecution, Bota was compromised by a channel someone else controlled. Skype was Microsoft’s channel, and it was tapped. The bank account was the state’s channel, and it froze donors and delivered their names to the secret service. Social media was subject to local jurisdiction, and its in-country representative took down posts. Each tool had a third party in the middle, and the third party could be pressured. Logos is a stack for building applications where there is no third party to pressure: private, censorship-resistant messaging; decentralised storage and file transfer; a blockchain that protects the privacy of participants, including the people who operate it; and a mixnet underneath so that observers can’t see who is talking to whom. No in-country representatives, no centralised web server, no one able to freeze or revoke accounts or messages. None of this would have saved her from a decade of persecution – a regime that will torture your brother has options beyond digital protocols – but it was specific, technical failures in centralised services that gave them their opening: an intercepted call, a surveilled donor list, a removable post. Those are solvable. Bota remains a strong advocate of privacy-preserving technology. Returning to the topic of the EU’s chat control regulation, she said the bill’s passage was a bad precedent but not the end, that European citizens can still fight before it becomes a permanent system, and that this fight is exactly where human rights defenders and developers need each other. Watch the full interview . For more on Logos and how to get involved,  follow us on X .
